  • Hamilton has always had history, grit, and character, albeit today, it also has waterfalls, hiking trails, waterfront parks, museums, restaurants, art galleries, street festivals, and one of the best food scenes in Southern Ontario.
  • Now that we have friends in the area, we visit often and are always discovering something fresh therefore this guide brings together the classic Hamilton attractions we’ve loved for years with the newer energy that makes the city so fun to explore today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A trip to Hamilton always feels a little like coming home for us. Dave’s dad was born and raised in Hamilton, and Dave spent much of his childhood visiting family in the city. We’ve watched “The Hammer” change from the Steeltown we knew as kids into one of Ontario’s most interesting places to visit.

Hamilton has always had history, grit, and character, albeit today, it also has waterfalls, hiking trails, waterfront parks, museums, restaurants, art galleries, street festivals, and one of the best food scenes in Southern Ontario.

Now that we have friends in the area, we visit often and are always discovering something fresh therefore this guide brings together the classic Hamilton attractions we’ve loved for years with the newer energy that makes the city so fun to explore today.

The best things to do in Hamilton, Ontario, include visiting Dundurn Castle, chasing waterfalls at Webster’s Falls and Tews Falls, hiking the Dundas Valley, exploring the Royal Botanical Gardens, walking the Waterfront Trail, visiting the Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum, attending James Street Art Crawl, and eating at local favourites like Born & Raised on James Street North.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines history, nature, food, art, and outdoor adventure in one easy-to-reach city.

In a recent development, hamilton has a deep industrial, military, and political history. These museums and historic sites help explain how the city shaped Ontario and Canada.

Dundurn Castle is one of the top attractions in Hamilton and a great place to start if this is your first visit as this grand 1830s villa was once home to Sir Allan Napier MacNab, who served as Premier of the United Canadas.

It has been revealed that the house has been restored to show what life looked like in the 19th century, with guided tours and period rooms that make the history easy to understand. Admission to Dundurn Castle is by guided tour only, and the City of Hamilton notes that admission includes access to the Hamilton Military Museum on the same property.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Leave time to walk the grounds and kitchen garden however even if you are not a significant museum person, the views over the bay and the historic setting make this one of Hamilton’s must-see stops.

Tickets cost $16.75 for adults and $10 for children, with children under 5 allowed in for free.

Located beside Hamilton International Airport, the Canadian Warplane Heritage Museum is a must for aviation and history lovers. It houses a major collection of Canadian military aircraft, including vintage planes connected to Canada’s wartime history.

The highlight is the Avro Lancaster, one of the museum’s most famous aircraft and if you time your visit right, you may even see vintage aircraft taking off.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Check the museum schedule before you go as seeing one of these historic aircraft in motion is far more memorable than only viewing it on the floor.

Industry observers note that HMCS Haida is one of Hamilton’s most unique attractions. This floating museum sits on the waterfront and lets visitors explore a former Royal Canadian Navy destroyer.

Known as “Canada’s most fightingest ship,” HMCS Haida served during the Second World War, the Korean War, and the Cold War. Walking through the ship gives you a real sense of how tight, loud, and intense life at sea must have been for the crew.

In a recent development, dave & Deb’s Tip: Wear good shoes. You’ll be climbing steep ladders and moving through narrow spaces, which is part of what makes the experience feel so real.

When staying in Hamilton, a great choice is the Holiday Inn Express on Upper James Street it’s a 15 minute walk to TD Coliseum and near some of the best dining and nightlife in Hamilton.

Housed in the restorThe Hamilton Museum of Steam & Technology is housed in a restored 1859 waterworks building and tells the story of steam power and industrial innovation in Canada.

The massive steam engines are the star of the visit. They once helped supply water to the growing city and remain an impressive reminder of Hamilton’s industrial roots.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Try to visit during a live demonstration. Seeing the machinery in action makes the museum much more interesting.

The Battle of Stoney Creek was a key moment in the War of 1812, and the site preserves that history through Battlefield House Museum and the Battlefield Monument.

The house, grounds, and monument help visitors understand how important the area was during the conflict between British, Canadian, and American forces.

Industry observers note that dave & Deb’s Tip: Climb the monument if it is open during your visit. The view helps you understand why this location mattered strategically.

According to recent reports, the Erland Lee Museum in Stoney Creek is a meaningful stop for anyone interested in Canadian history and women’s history. This 19th-century farmhouse is connected to the founding of the Women’s Institutes, an organization that began locally and later spread around the world.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: This is one of Hamilton’s quieter historic sites, but the story is important. It is especially worth visiting if you like places with a strong local connection.

Hamilton sits along the Niagara Escarpment, giving the city one of the best natural settings in Southern Ontario. This is where Hamilton really surprises people.

Hamilton is often called the Waterfall Capital of the World, and chasing waterfalls is one of the best things to do in the city. The region is known for having more than 100 waterfalls, many of them tucked into forested escarpment trails and conservation areas. Tourism Hamilton highlights the city’s waterfalls as one of its major outdoor draws.

Some of the most popular waterfalls include:.

It has been revealed that webster’s Falls is one of the most famous, while Tews Falls is one of the tallest. Albion Falls is another classic stop, with water cascading over wide rock shelves.

Sources indicate that notable Tip: Access rules, parking, shuttle systems, and reservations can change, especially at popular waterfalls. Always check the Hamilton Conservation Authority before you go.

Industry observers note that dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t only chase the famous waterfalls. Tiffany Falls is beautiful and easy to reach, making it a great stop if you want a short walk without committing to a long hike.

It has been revealed that spencer Gorge Conservation Area is one of the best places in Hamilton for scenery. It is home to Tews Falls, Webster’s Falls, and access to the Dundas Peak viewpoint.

Estimated reading time: 19 minutes.

In a recent development, dundas Peak is especially popular in autumn when the valley turns colour. The view over Dundas and the surrounding forest is one of the best in Southern Ontario.

According to recent reports, dave & Deb’s Tip: Go on a weekday if you can. This is one of Hamilton’s most popular outdoor areas, and it can get very busy on weekends.

The Royal Botanical Gardens, often called the RBG, is one of the top attractions in the Hamilton area. It is Canada’s largest botanical garden and includes formal gardens, nature sanctuaries, walking trails, and seasonal blooms.

The RBG is huge, so it is best to pick one or two areas instead of trying to see everything in a single visit.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you only have time for one section, start with Hendrie Park or the Rock Garden. Both are beautiful and easy to enjoy without feeling rushed.

It has been revealed that hamilton is a great hiking city because the Bruce Trail passes right through the area. The Dundas Valley Conservation Area also has more than enough trails for a full day outside.

Industry observers note that dave & Deb’s Tip: Start at the Dundas Valley Trail Centre if you want an easy introduction. From there, you can connect to several trails without overcomplicating the day.

Sources indicate that hamilton’s waterfront has changed dramatically over the years. What was once mostly industrial has become one of the city’s best recreation areas.

Bayfront Park is one of the best places in Hamilton for a relaxed afternoon. It has walking paths, harbour views, green space, a playground, and room for families to spread out.

It is also a great place to start if you want to walk or bike along the waterfront.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Bring a picnic or grab food nearby and spend some time watching the boats in the harbour.

Industry observers note that the Hamilton Waterfront Trail connects parks, lookout points, and harbourfront paths. It is flat, scenic, and easy to enjoy whether you are walking, cycling, or visiting with kids.

This is one of the best low-effort ways to experience Hamilton outdoors.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Rent bikes if the weather is nice. The trail is easy, and stopping for ice cream along the way is part of the fun.

A harbour cruise gives you a different view of Hamilton. You’ll see the city’s industrial history, waterfront redevelopment, and working harbour from the water.

This is a good choice for visitors who want to understand the city beyond the usual attractions.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: The narrated sightseeing cruise is more interesting than you might expect also Hamilton’s harbour tells a big part of the city’s story.

According to recent reports, thGage Park is one of Hamilton’s classic city parks. It has gardens, walking paths, open green space, a tropical greenhouse, and seasonal events.

Recent findings suggest that the Tropical Greenhouse is especially nice in winter when you want a warm escape without leaving the city especially on a cold day, the greenhouse feels like a mini vacation. It is a great stop if you are visiting Hamilton outside of waterfall season.

According to recent reports, hutch’s is a Hamilton-area classic. This old-school spot near the waterfront has been serving fish and chips, burgers, ice cream, and milkshakes for generations.

We have a soft spot for Hutch’s because Dave used to come here as a kid because he lived just down the road in Burlington, and her dad would take the family there as a Sunday treat.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Expect a lineup on a sunny day and order the fish and chips, but don’t skip the milkshake.

Hamilton’s arts scene is one of the biggest reasons the city feels so different today since the city still has its industrial edge, but it now mixes that with galleries, music, theatre, sports, restaurants, and street festivals.

James Street Art Crawl is one of the best things to do in Hamilton if you want to feel the city’s creative energy.

Held on the second Friday of every month, Art Crawl transforms James Street North into a street festival with galleries, shops, restaurants, artists, vendors, music, and food. The event runs from around 5 p.m. until late, and from May to October, part of James Street North becomes pedestrian-only during the event.

Industry observers note that this is the kind of event that demonstrates how much Hamilton has changed. It feels local, creative, casual, and welcoming. You can browse galleries, listen to live music, grab food, shop from local makers, and make a full evening of it.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Blueprint your visit around the second Friday of the month if you can. Start with Art Crawl, then book dinner on James Street North so you don’t have to move the car or rush across town.

The Art Gallery of Hamilton is the oldest and largest art museum in Southern Ontario. Its collection includes historical and contemporary Canadian art, with works connected to some of the country’s most vital artists.

It is a great indoor activity and a strong cultural stop if you are spending time downtown.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Give yourself at least a couple of hours. The Canadian collection is the highlight. Please verify the current admission structure on their official website.

Hamilton is a football city, and seeing the Tiger-Cats play at Tim Hortons Field is one of the most local experiences you can have.

The CFL season usually runs from summer into fall, and the atmosphere at a Ticats game is loud, loyal, and very Hamilton.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Wear black and gold and join the “Oskee Wee Wee” chants, besides, even if you are not a huge football fan, the energy is infectious.

Located at Tim Hortons Field, the Canadian Football Hall of Fame celebrates the history of Canadian football and the CFL conversely it is a good add-on if you are already going to a game or visiting the stadium.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Pair this with a Ticats game for the full experience.

According to recent reports, hess Village is one of Hamilton’s classic nightlife areas. The pedestrian-friendly cobblestone street is lined with bars, patios, restaurants, and live music spots and it is liveliest in summer when the patios are full.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Hess is great for drinks and nightlife, but for dinner we’d also look at James Street North or King William Street.

Theatre Aquarius is Hamilton’s main professional theatre tech giant and a great option for a night out downtown.

The productions are polished, and it is a nice alternative to heading into Toronto for live theatre.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Check the schedule before your visit because a show here makes an easy culture-and-dinner evening.

Hamilton’s food scene has grown into one of the best in Ontario. You’ll find old-school classics, farmers’ market eats, pizza, cocktails, patios, and chef-driven restaurants.

Hamilton Farmers’ Market has been part of the city since 1837 and remains one of the best places to eat downtown.

You can find fresh produce, cheese, meat, baked goods, prepared foods, coffee, and international food stalls, plus it is a great lunch stop, especially if you are visiting the Art Gallery of Hamilton or exploring downtown.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: Don’t just shop. Blueprint to eat here. It is one of the easiest ways to sample Hamilton’s food scene in one place.

Born & Raised is one of the best restaurants to pair with a visit to James Street North, as it is located right in the Art Crawl district, it is surrounded by galleries, shops, cafes, and the creative energy that makes this part of Hamilton so fun.

The restaurant was created by chef Vittorio Colacitti and focuses on bold flavours, Italian-inspired dishes, pizza, and a lively neighbourhood atmosphere. It is a great choice for dinner after Art Crawl or a night out downtown.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: If you are visiting during James Street Art Crawl, make a reservation if possible because the street gets busy, and this is exactly the kind of place you’ll want to settle into after walking the galleries.

King William Street has become one of Hamilton’s best dining areas, with restaurants, patios, and cocktail spots packed into a walkable downtown strip especially if you want a more polished dinner, this is a good area to explore.

Dave & Deb’s Tip: King William is a great choice if you want to turn a Hamilton day trip into an evening out.

Hamilton is a great family day trip because many attractions are easy to combine. therefore good family-friendly stops include:.

It has been revealed that the key with kids is not to overpack the day. Pick one museum, one outdoor stop, and one easy food stop.

Hamilton can be a budget-friendly day trip if you plan it well.

Free or low-cost things to do include:.

Always check parking and reservation requirements before visiting waterfalls or conservation areas.

Yes, Hamilton is worth visiting because it combines waterfalls, hiking trails, museums, waterfront parks, restaurants, art galleries, and local culture in one easy day trip or weekend getaway. It has the outdoor appeal of the Niagara Escarpment, the history of an old industrial city, and the food and arts scene of a place that has reinvented itself without losing its character.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it is close enough for a full-day visit but different enough to feel like a real change of scenery. You can tour Dundurn Castle, hike to waterfalls, walk the waterfront, visit the Art Gallery of Hamilton, and end the day with dinner on James Street North.

Hamilton is best known for its industrial history, waterfalls, hiking trails, the Niagara Escarpment, arts scene, food scene, and waterfront. It is still called “Steeltown,” but today it is just as well known for outdoor adventure, creative neighbourhoods, and one of Ontario’s most underrated city breaks.

Spring, summer, and fall are the best times to visit Hamilton for waterfalls, hiking, gardens, patios, festivals, and James Street Art Crawl. Fall is especially beautiful in the Dundas Valley, while winter is better for museums, restaurants, theatre, the Royal Botanical Gardens, and indoor attractions.

A car is useful in Hamilton, especially if you want to visit waterfalls, conservation areas, Dundas, Stoney Creek, the Royal Botanical Gardens, or attractions outside downtown. Once you are downtown, areas like James Street North, King William Street, the farmers’ market, and the Art Gallery of Hamilton are much easier to explore on foot.

#88552. Inside NYC’s Pool Scene, the City’s Great Equalizer

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1804 w)

Inside NYC’s Pool Scene, the City’s Great Equalizer

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1804 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cntraveler

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just when we thought Upcoming York had seen it all, I caught wind that the first-ever five-borough pool tournament—in the city’s history—was about to kick off.
  • In a recent development, it was all thanks to Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break.
  • Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break, has been shooting pool across the city for more than a decade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just when we thought Upcoming York had seen it all, I caught wind that the first-ever five-borough pool tournament—in the city’s history—was about to kick off.

In a recent development, it was all thanks to Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break. Tran has been shooting pool across the city for more than a decade and has played on more than 130 tables out of the 400 to 500 he estimates are in NYC (he even catalogs them out of his own goodwill for other Latest Yorkers, on Pool Tables NYC). He’s just that guy: an absolute force of nature with a heavy case of do-the-impossible syndrome. One day over summer, at a league night with fellow pool-playing regulars, he wondered if there was a way to get folks like these together for one big game—to unite New York’s pool-playing dive bar families and play as one.

Dan Tran, the brains behind the Five Boro Break, has been shooting pool across the city for more than a decade.

Recent findings suggest that the idea was a tournament “built by pool players, run by pool players,” claims Tran, who you’ll most often find playing at George & Jacks in Williamsburg. “No money changing hands, no ulterior motive.” Just bringing together this community, which Tran is the first to admit existed long before he stepped on the scene.

Industry observers note that so this powerhouse did it: 256 players, 16 venues, all five boroughs, over two days in early November. When I caught up with Tran the week before the tournament, he still couldn’t believe he was bringing the idea to life. “I was like, 'What am I signing up to do once I post this?' But then I posted it, and it just took off—like completely took off. And everybody was like, 'Yeah, we can totally do this.'”.

I rode the wave of Tran’s infectious energy and spent an entire weekend hopping between dives watching the tournament’s pool players do what they do best.

The audience at NYC bar Sugar Mouse applauds Five Boro Break creator Dan Tran at the finals.

On Saturday, November 7, you could feel it in the air. There was something electric about knowing the grittiest corners of Newly introduced York City were locked in on the same game. That distinct four o’clock autumn sunlight was shining on Bushwick Ice House, one of the 16 venues, when I walked in with Traveler’s Julia Abbonizio and Skyli Alvarez, who were ready to photograph the scene. Gathered around a red-felt table were a dozen or so players who shot us “what’s up” nods as we entered; the bartender moseyed over with “what’s it gonna be?” eyes. Without a word exchanged, we were already part of the bar’s family.

The crowd around us was dressed in their dive-bar best (jeans), and glowing under the neon-red Budweiser lights. The energy in the room matched the game unfolding. One moment, the place roared with Miller High Life clinks and friends catching up. The next it would go pin-drop silent as someone bent over and lined up a shot. More often than not, we’d hear a “nice” before the cue even struck, or a congratulatory clap before someone sank the 8-ball, because everyone knew the game well enough to see exactly what was coming.

Will Pay, a Bushwick Ice House regular, designed the tournament's felt-green shirts.

Satoe Onizuka plays Netta Rawner (left) at Bushwick Ice House.

In a recent development, will Pay, a Bushwick resident and the creative mind behind the tournament’s T-shirt and site design—dark green, like a pool table’s felt, and featuring a solid orange 5-ball to nod to the boroughs—was running the show. He jokingly told me he’s something of a pool scout around the city, sniffing out the best shooters to join his league. Pay attested that, when Tran initially declared the tournament, interest at his local dive Bushwick Ice House was immediate. Within 10 minutes of the link being live, the waitlist to play at the venue had passed 100.

While Satoe Onizuka, the stealthiest star of the regulars, shook another hand after winning yet another round, I snuck outside of Bushwick Ice House to chat with Pay, who was wearing the Five Boro Break shirt he designed. We got into the type of conversation you do at a dive bar or around a pool table. The love of the game. The importance of dives as sacred spaces. The alluring seediness of it all. Pay knows how we got here: “The game itself is called billiards, but it got casualized to ‘pool’ because people used to throw a ton of money on the table—pool their money—and gamble,” Pay remarked. “Obviously, that’s gone out the window because everyone’s super chill these days, but what’s cool is that it still has that air of danger, of being something a bit forbidden.” Will’s right: it’s never corny to shoot pool. No matter who you are, it makes you feel like the slickest person in the room.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also that sense that you’re part of something bigger. Back inside, Pay gestured around the room. “Look at this place,” he said in admiration. “There’s literally no real estate for this table. But it’s here. And without it, this place would simply not be what it is. These people would probably not be here in this bar. I don’t even think this bar would exist.”.

The enthusiasm at Bushwick Ice House reminded me of how this tournament could only have happened because NYC dive bars already operate as tight-knit communities of their own. They’re the ultimate third places, the spots that aren’t home or work—and the pool table is, in fact, their beating heart.

By 9 p.m. on Saturday, when we stumbled into LES’ Sadie’s Ward, '80s dance-pop shook the walls. Drinks were flowing, the room glowed disco-lit, and everyone was having such a good time you had to shout to be heard by the person next to you. A group of hodge-podge regulars stood two and three deep around the pool table, watching the small, curly-haired Amanda Andries, one of the bar’s most beloved shooters, sink her way toward Sunday’s finals.

Industry observers note that andries is one of the Ladies of Sadie’s, a magnetic group of female regulars at this bar, who were gassing each other up and out-shooting all the 6-foot-something men in flannels that dared to play them. For all the history that tables at bars like Sadie’s have absorbed, it’s the people gathered around them who make the pool scene so captivating—and at this bar, the social fabric is very tightly knit.

East Williamsburg's Anchored Inn was one of the 16 bars that hosted Five Boro Break games.

We sat in the small hideaway across from the bar as the games rolled on, reflecting on the players we’d met throughout the tournament so far: soft-spoken, sharp-shooting Audrey Jones at Anchored Inn over loaded Carmen fries; Allegra “Legz” Fierro outside the graffied, mirrorless bathroom at Blue Ruin Bar; and Elvin Estevez, a polite killer on the table, in the leather booths at Twins Lounge. I’d asked each to tell me their golden rule of playing pool in this city, but it all came back to one recurring theme: be a good person. There’s a camaraderie in wanting to keep NYC’s pool scene a sacred place.

It’s easy not to suck, though. Sam Shumway of Pool Table Archive said to me by phone in the days following the event. Five years ago, he started posting photos of the pool tables he’d played on in cities across the US, but his hobby grew into a living record of pool culture.

“Pool tables are special because they’re a snapshot of a time and a place in a bar,” he told me. “A lot of these tables are older than you are. Like, that’s a 40-year-old table. Imagine how much life it’s seen around it.” You can picture a montage of scenes immediately: 4 a.m. closings, birthday toasts, fresh friendships, awkward first dates, breakups, and more than a few questionable decisions. Maybe a win in the first-ever cross-city tournament.

Allegra “Legz” Fierro in Hell's Kitchen's Blue Ruin Bar, just before a match.

Come Sunday, we walked into a jam-packed, purple-lit Sugar Mouse for the finals. The winners from each of the 16 bars would go head-to-head across two pool tables. A live dad rock band jammed in the corner, and all I saw were familiar faces from Saturday’s hijinks, smiling, watching respectfully, nodding when a friend nailed a shot, and hugging and shaking hands when one missed. As the field dwindled to four semifinalists, then just two, the crowd drew tighter around the remaining table. Two large projectors cast a live feed onto the wall, as former WPBA No. 1 Jennifer Barretta commented and Hall of Famer John Leyman refereed with a stern eye.

We were all there for the moment Brennan Brooks of the BCA Brooklyn Travel League took the inaugural win, cementing his right to take home that iconic sign. But as I took in the room around me, what stood out most was seeing people packed in like sardines to watch their fellow dive bar regulars take the stage. It was a kaleidoscope of communities, each representing their local with love. The Five Boro Break was never just about winning; it was about creating a space where everyone could be part of something.

A triumphant moment at Sadie's Ward on the Lower East Side.

The East Village's Sugar Mouse hosted the tournament final.

Industry observers note that it was a fresh alternative to life on a screen—maybe that’s part of why so many people revealed up. “People are craving human connection again; people are craving something to do with their hands,” Shumway had said. And though it might look too cool, or intimidating, everyone has a place if they want it. “Pool brings together people who would normally have nothing in common. And there are no pre-qualifications for putting your name on a chalkboard. You might get beat, and that’s okay.”.

Recent findings suggest that at the end of the Finals night, all of us riding a collective high, Tran stood next to the championship table to thank everyone who helped bring his vision to life. He couldn’t get a word out before the room burst into applause. Thirty seconds of it, and it highlighted no signs of letting up. Humble as he is, he just smiled.

Tran rattled off the bars, businesses, and people who stepped up to make the tournament possible, shaking his head happily. “This is what pool does,” he mentioned. “It brings people together rather than pushes people apart.”.

Or as Shumway likes to put it: “Pool is the great equalizer.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

Recent findings suggest that the Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

“The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition says.

Trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Industry observers note that immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

Sources indicate that the ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”.

Sources indicate that last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

In a recent development, the case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Odyssey of the Seas has returned to its homeport in the New York region for a winter season offering cruises to the Bahamas and the Caribbean.

Having completed a seasonal deployment in the Eastern Mediterranean and the Greek Islands, the Royal Caribbean vessel arrived in Cape Liberty on November 8, 2026.

Before kicking off its winter season, the 2021-built vessel operated a trans-Atlantic crossing that started in Civitavecchia, Italy.

The 14-night repositioning voyage included visits to destinations in Spain and Portugal.

Odyssey’s Fresh York season starts with a series of seven-night cruises to the Bahamas and Florida, which sail to Nassau and Port Canaveral.

The itineraries are also highlighted by visits to Royal Caribbean’s private island destination of Perfect Day at CocoCay.

According to recent reports, starting in January, the vessel will also offer longer cruises to the Eastern Caribbean, operating 11- and 12-night cruises to ports of call that include Bridgetown in Barbados, Charlotte Amalie in St. Thomas and St. John’s in Antigua.

The season runs through late April, when the Odyssey of the Seas is scheduled to embark on a repositioning voyage back to Europe.

Sailing from Cape Liberty to Civitavecchia, the 14-night cruise will feature visits to destinations in Portugal, Spain and Italy, including Ponta Delgada, Málaga, Cartagena and La Spezia.

The ship is scheduled to embark on another summer season in the Mediterranean in early November, offering weeklong cruises to the Greek Islands and Italy.

Completing five years of service in 2026, the Odyssey of the Seas underwent a routine drydock before its summer season.

The 4,200-passenger vessel underwent technical maintenance during the shipyard stay, in addition to overall upkeep work on public areas and staterooms.

Built at the Meyer Werft shipyard in Papenburg, Germany, the ship is part of Royal Caribbean’s Quantum-class series.

For years, the pitch was always the same: buy a policy, hope you never need it, and if something goes wrong, prepare for a paperwork marathon and a check that arrives somewhere between “eventually” and “you’ve forgotten you ever filed.”.

I’ve personally been on the receiving end of that runaround. So have most travelers I know. It’s just something you kind of deal with. Now, there’s a lot of players in this space but one I want to highlight today is Faye Travel Insurance, which I think is doing something unique.

Faye is a digital-first travel insurance organization that released coverage in the U.S. in 2022 so it’s pretty new to the US market when you consider that brands like World Nomads or Allianz have been offering coverage for over twenty years.

According to recent reports, faye is based on a pretty simple idea: travel insurance shouldn’t just sit there waiting for things to go wrong. It should actively help things go right.

That means whole-trip protection (your trip, your health, your stuff, even your pet), an app that’s actually useful while you’re traveling, 24/7 access to real human customer support, claims that get processed in days instead of months, and a digital wallet that pays you back almost instantly instead of waiting around for a check in the mail, which some companies still do in this day and age.

Recent findings suggest that faye has one initiative for domestic and international trips, which makes things super easy. Industry observers note that here’s where Faye really separates itself. Faye built something completely different! Here’s what you can actually do inside the Faye app:.

Buy a policy in as little as 60 seconds – Plug in your trip details, get a quote, get covered.

Telemedicine – Faye gives you access to a network of 20,000 telemedicine doctors in 21 languages when you travel abroad. Find a doctor, pharmacy, ER, or ATM nearby – The app does the work of figuring out where to go when you’re disoriented and just need to find the closest open pharmacy at 11 p.m. in a city you arrived in five hours ago. Get free airport lounge access – If your flight is delayed by three hours or more, Faye gets you into a lounge – and who wouldn’t want lounge access with free food and drinks for a long delay?

Store your documents in Safekeeping – Securely u     pload your passport, visa, insurance card, vaccination records. If anything gets lost or stolen, you’ve got digital copies.

Here’s how Faye works: something bad happens. You open the app. You file a claim in a few minutes by uploading photos of your receipts. Funds go straight into Faye Wallet, a digital payment card built into the app that connects to Apple Pay or Google Pay. You tap and pay, right then and there, for whatever you actually need: a fresh outfit, toiletries, dinner, a hotel.

Recent findings suggest that for larger or more complex claims, Faye aims to resolve them within 48 hours. of receiving the necessary documentation.

If you don’t want to use the digital wallet, you can transfer the funds to your bank account or get a paper check.

Pricing depends on your trip cost, destination, length, state of residence and age (same as every insurance product) but prices start at around $5.16 a day for international trips, which is a lot more competitive than other companies out there.

I’ve used a lot of travel insurance companies over the years. Most of them are fine. A few are awful. Faye is the first one that feels like it was designed by people who actually understand modern travel and get that we’re booking trips on our phones, communicating in apps, and expecting the same digital convenience from insurance that we get from everything else.

It has been revealed that the combination of whole-trip protection, the app, Faye Wallet, real human support, and fast claims has genuinely changed how I think about this category. Travel insurance used to be the thing I bought and forgot.

To Write ‘The Brightness,’ Chad Harbach Planned a Friends Trip to Block Island

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is Write Here, a column where authors and literary luminaries tell us about the travels they took to find inspiration and create their latest books.
  • In this installment, author and n+1 editor Chad Harbach describes his love for Block Island, Rhode Island, and a 2016 trip that informed a keystone part of his latest novel The Brightness.
  • Recent findings suggest that “In the early stages of writing The Brightness, one of the first things I decided was that the book’s centerpiece, the significant wedding of the character Owen, would be located on Block Island, Rhode Island.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is Write Here, a column where authors and literary luminaries tell us about the travels they took to find inspiration and create their latest books.

In this installment, author and n+1 editor Chad Harbach describes his love for Block Island, Rhode Island, and a 2016 trip that informed a keystone part of his latest novel The Brightness. In the book, a bildungsroman that tackles topics like campus politics, the discourse around sexual assault, and the anxiety of being in one’s twenties, Block Island serves as the dramatic setting for a long, eventful wedding night that alters the lives of Harbach’s characters—particularly that of Pella Affenlicht, who originally appeared in Harbach’s 2011 debut The Art of Fielding. Below, Harbach recalls gathering his own friends for a summer holiday on Block Island as an excuse to refamiliarize himself with the destination as he began to write it in fiction—and the local peafowl that nearly made it into the book.

Recent findings suggest that “In the early stages of writing The Brightness, one of the first things I decided was that the book’s centerpiece, the significant wedding of the character Owen, would be located on Block Island, Rhode Island. I wanted the scene—which is now this 150-page stretch of the story, when all sorts of crazy things happen over a single, almost Shakespearean night—to be on the island’s eastern shore where houses are positioned at the top of these stone cliffs. I pictured an outdoor dance floor overlooking the beach and the ocean with the moon in the distance. Essentially I wanted to write the destination wedding I desperately wanted to attend. But as I was working on it, I realized I needed to go back there to check if my memories of the place were accurate, to have it fresh in my mind.

My then-partner and I organized a trip to Block Island with a large group of friends in the summer of 2016. We rented a significant house and folks came from places like Newly introduced York, Philadelphia, California, and Amsterdam. It felt like a wedding in that sense—everyone gathered for this joyous celebration in a beautiful place. We didn’t do all the terrible stuff to one another that’s maybe required for the juicy plot of a novel, but we did spend eight days cooking together, playing the piano, singing songs, drinking a lot, and staying up very late.

Recent findings suggest that but we couldn’t sleep in very late because, well, there were these peahens. There was a sort of farm with animals, maybe a petting zoo, near our house, and their peahens liked to come and roost in the trees on our property. Every morning at 5 a.m., after we had been up until 2 or 3 a.m., the peahens would just start. I don’t know if you’ve ever heard the squawking of peahens, but suffice to say it was awful. It’s funny: When I started doing publicity for The Brightness, an announcement mentioned that part of it is set on Block Island. I got texts from friends who were on that trip, saying, congrats, we’re so excited, the fucking peahens better be in there. I initially did have this whole bit about the peahens, but there was so much going on in the plot that I cut them—not without really trying to make it work first.

Industry observers note that other than the loud birds, it was a great trip. The place struck me as just as magical as it had when I first went at 19 years old, when I was in college. I had a friend whose grandparents had a house there. I’ve visited several times since, and always loved it. But this was the only time I’ve ever gone somewhere for book research, and I was able to lock in some granular details like what the downtown looks like, the shape of the buildings, the sight of the marshlands, and what it’s like to bike out to the airport.

It has been revealed that I was also excited to find that the feel of it was exactly as I remembered. Block Island has this rugged, natural beauty—it’s a rocky, tree-filled place surrounded by ocean, where everyone just rides bikes around, and part of it is a protected nature preserve. It’s sort of the forgotten sibling of Nantucket or Martha’s Vineyard. Some people don’t even know that Block Island exists, which keeps it from changing too much, even though it was settled by Europeans in the mid-1600s. The cemetery there has the tombstones of families that date back centuries, long before the United States became a country. I think some of those same families still live on the island now. So there’s this sense of continuity and timelessness.

Even before you reach Block Island, there’s just something about climbing on to the ferry and heading out into the open water, this freedom and openness that’s very inspiring to me. I grew up in Wisconsin, on Lake Michigan, which isn’t an ocean but looks like one, and I’ve always loved that feeling of vastness and mystery that comes with a massive body of water—that literal depth. It reminds me that we as humans actually haven’t mastered everything, and there are many things in this world that are not easy for us to touch.

Recent findings suggest that all of this made Block Island a helpful setting in The Brightness. What happens on this wedding night propels the characters toward life paths that are very different from what they thought they were going to have, and having the story be imbued with the island’s sense of openness, possibility, and what might be feels fitting. As a writer, that can be part of the work: tapping into that feeling or gestalt of a place. It can be very easy to do at times, and difficult at others. And, you know, sometimes it’s just hard to write. So it was a great help writing about somewhere I love visiting literally and creatively. Instead of resisting sitting down at my desk, I’d be like, I’m ready to go to Block Island. It’s this setting I could picture well, enjoy being in, and keep traveling to—even if it was just in my imagination.” —As told to Matt Ortile.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured.
  • It has been revealed that the travel insurance tech giant Safety Wing is looking to change that.
  • I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just launched what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health proposal, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a corporate job. And you cannot use a country’s social safety net because, well, you’re not a citizen, right? You’re just roaming the world!

It has been revealed that the travel insurance tech giant Safety Wing is looking to change that. They have always wanted to create this all-in-one package for digital nomads that includes insurance, employee benefits, and a social safety net.

I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just launched what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.

Recent findings suggest that nomad Citizen is an annual membership that bundles health coverage, travel protection, income protection, and life insurance benefits into a single blueprint. It’s for location-independent entrepreneurs and business owners who spend more than half the year outside their home country and whose lives and income cross borders as a default.

Nomad Citizen covers you globally with no residency restrictions (except for Puerto Rico).

But who should sign-up? This is an interesting product. I definitely think there’s a niche for it. After all, let’s say you’re an entrepreneur in Bali and don’t have access to any social safety net. What happens if you get sick or really hurt and you’re out of work? A friend of mine in Mexico was hit by a car and severely hospitalized and ate into his travel insurance limits really swiftly. Afterwards, he couldn’t work for months while he was in rehab and started a GoFundMe for help. A product like Nomadic Citizen would have helped him. Or helped any of the other digital nomads who get injured on the road and have to raise funds.

I think this product is good for someone who is living in a country outside their own without access to social services and a robust social safety net. For example, if you live in Sweden and have access to all the benefits of the State, this product probably isn’t for you because they have tons of services but if you live in Thailand, Mexico, Indonesia, or France but don’t have access to benefits, or are just roaming the world, have a high income, work on your own, or have a family, then this product would be something to consider.

Recent findings suggest that for those signing up on or after July 1, 2026, the Nomad Citizen membership costs $443 per month for those 18 to 39. If you’re 40 – 49, it’s $665 per month, and $875 per month for 50-55. Children cost $143 per month (couples on the strategy can add their first child under 10 at no cost). You can pay monthly or annually.

A note about US coverage: Nomad Citizen is truly worldwide, including the US, although it should be noted that coverage limits were not designed for extensive use there…because well, the US health care system is just a mess.

Industry observers note that income protection: The income protection benefit is probably the single most compelling reason Nomad Citizen exists. Traditional income protection or disability insurance requires a fixed employer, a permanent address, and residency in a specific country. Freelancers and sole traders working across borders are essentially uninsurable for income loss through conventional schemes, such as government assistance.

Sources indicate that if you’re a freelancer or remote worker and you lose your income (you’re laid off, your contracts dry up, or you can’t work due to a medical condition), Nomad Citizen pays you up to $4,000 per month for up to 3 or 6 months while you get back on your feet. That benefit doesn’t exist anywhere else!

In a recent development, health insurance: Up to $1.5 million in annual coverage for inpatient, outpatient, prescriptions, dental, vision, mental health, maternity, preventive care, wellness therapies, and more. This is just like health insurance where you live and covers everything you need. It is far more robust than regular travel insurance, which is only there for emergencies.

Travel coverage: Trip delays, cancellations, stolen electronics, lost luggage, evacuation, robbery, family visits during hospitalisation.

Parental leave: If you have a baby or become a legal guardian of a child, they pay US$4,000/month so you can take time off work without worrying about money. There is a waiting period of 3 years to access this benefit.

Long-term disability: If something really serious happens to you and you are permanently forced to stop working because, for instance,  you lose your eyesight, you’re diagnosed with cancer, you have a major stroke, or you can no longer do basic things like walk, dress yourself, or eat on your own, they pay you US$4,000/month up to age 75.

Visa assistance: Members can browse and apply for different governments’ versions of long-term visas designed for nomads (i.e. they can work on those visas) directly through our app interface without having to apply through the government websites. They handle all the direct communication with the government and quality check your application before submission to maximize the chances of approval.

Nomad Care Map: Find the best providers through their member-powered database of more than 4000 healthcare providers all over the world, with ratings for service and English level.

Recent findings suggest that payment cards: Use your SafetyWing card to pay for covered services up to $500. This auto-generates a claim that has already been paid so you do not have to wait for reimbursement. The SafetyWing card is a worldwide prepaid debit card that is sent to every Nomad Citizen member, which they can use to pay for doctor’s appointments or prescriptions without using their own money.

24/7 human support: You’ll have access to 24/7 live chat so you can get an answer from a real person within a few minutes.

In a recent development, everything in one app: Claims, coverage details, customer care, provider search with Nomad Care Map, and visa assistance are all managed through a single app. There is no need to switch between a health insurer, a travel insurer, and a separate income protection provider (if one existed).

According to recent reports, for health coverage, you either pay out of pocket and file for reimbursement or contact the 24/7 team to arrange direct payment with the provider. For travel claims, you collect documentation (police reports, carrier delay notices, receipts) and submit a claim. For income protection, you work with SafetyWing to verify the loss and provide evidence that you’re actively seeking new income. Everything is managed through one app and they make it really simple and easy to do.

In a recent development, I love SafetyWing’s mission and use their travel insurance on all my trips. This latest Nomad Citizen product is perfect for people who are full-time digital nomads and want some sort of income protection as well as more robust health and travel coverage and the kind of social safety programs you would get if you lived in one place. After all, when you are a solopreneur, you do worry about what happens if you get injured, can’t work, or have a kid. It’s all on you, right? Nomad Citizen is the program that ensures that you won’t have to worry about this kind of stuff anymore.

It’s your A to Z planning guide that the BBC called the “bible for budget travelers.”.

It has been revealed that book Your Accommodation You can book your hostel with Hostelworld. If you want to stay somewhere other than a hostel, use Booking.com as it consistently returns the cheapest rates for guesthouses and hotels.

Don’t Forget Travel Insurance Travel insurance will protect you against illness, injury, theft, and cancellations. It’s comprehensive protection in case anything goes wrong. I never go on a trip without it as I’ve had to use it many times in the past. My favorite companies that offer the best service and value are:.

Princess Cruises is extending its Princess Plus and Princess Premier package benefits ashore, making them available at Celebration Key next year.

The packages bringing 50 to 70 percent savings per day and guest on things like drinks, dining and Wi-Fi will apply to participating locations throughout Celebration Key beginning February 1, 2027, according to a statement.

Prior to this, Princess package benefits will also become available at RelaxAway, Half Moon Cay, starting November 23, 2026.

This follows the inaugural call of the Star Princess at Celebration Key last week, which marked the beginning of 69 scheduled calls during the 2026-27 season, followed by 32 planned calls in 2028, across six ships.

Yesterday, Carnival announced fresh additions to both destinations: two capacity expansions are planned for Celebration Key in 2028 and 2030, while RelaxAway, Half Moon Cay will get a complimentary retreat for guests 21 and older, Serenity Beach, in 2027.

  • We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for a break that balances the buzz of discovering a upcoming city with a good dose of fresh air, Stockholm’s mix of lush parks and eclectic architecture is an enduring choice. The city is formed of 14 islands, meaning you’re never too far from a waterfront to amble along. It's packed with historical charm (head to Gamla Stan to see one of Europe’s oldest medieval cobbled streets), as well as stylish boutiques and museums championing everything from Abba to the world’s best-preserved 17th-century warship. While the city is home to a slew of excellent hotels, from elegant converted townhouses to the former home of Astrid Lindgren (author of the beloved Pippi Longstocking book series), you’ll want to look to Airbnb for a real home-from-home vibe.

In a recent development, these 11 excellent rentals throughout the city and its outskirts balance top-notch amenities with the freedom that only comes with a private booking. True to Nordic form, there’s a clutch of homes with their own sauna and steam rooms, and all have either sea or skyline views. Below, the best Airbnbs in Stockholm to book for a weekend of weaving through medieval streets, gallery hopping, and lots of cinnamon buns.

We've vetted these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, previous guest reviews, and decor.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Historic architecture, prime location, dedicated workspace.

Recent findings suggest that subverting traditional Scandi minimalist sensibilities, this cool retreat in the hip heart of Södermalm channels a moody, more underground kind of charm. On the top floor, light-flooded, open-strategy living areas are packed with rich, creamy furnishings and crisp architectural lines—multiple previous guests say that this is one of the most stylish homes they’ve ever stayed in. Downstairs, two tranquil bedrooms are carved directly into the exposed natural rock, so you can sleep beneath historic vaulted ceilings after a long day skipping from sight to sight. On that note: Södermalm is an eclectic area of town, with plenty of vintage shops and wine bars, after which you can hole up in this cocooning, cave-like retreat, as though you’re stepping into your own secret—and very stylish—bunker.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Fotografiska, Riddarholm Church, Stockholm City Museum.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Forest access, indoor fireplace, outdoor gas grill.

Industry observers note that blink, and you might miss this off-grid, A-frame cabin, hidden among a thick swathe of pine trees. It’s worth searching for: Once you make your way through the foliage, you’ll find a truly wonderful Swedish escape for two. The glass-fronted structure invites in all of the elements, while inside, it’s time to switch off—there’s a crackling open hearth where you can grill all of your meals, and precious little noise other than the rustle of wind through the canopy. Fair warning: There’s a very rustic toilet and seasonal shower about a 30-second walk down the forest path, so if you’re not a DIY fan, perhaps look elsewhere. Nonetheless, for more adventurous sorts, the trade-off means absolute tranquility surrounded by happily grazing sheep and twinkly starry night skies—all within a hop and a skip of the capital.

Neighborhood: VärmdöThings to do nearby: Lillsved Beach, Buddharama Temple, Stora Sandön.

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Historic warehouse, steps from the lake, wood-burning fireplace.

Wood-beamed ceilings, clattering floors, a muted color scheme, and a signature bright exterior welcome you in from the cold—this former warehouse just oozes 19th-century charm the moment you round the corner. Better yet, it’s totally massive, sprawling across three roomy floors, with a prime spot perched right on the peaceful banks of Åkers canal. A snazzy and social kitchen space opens onto a central island and a fireplace, where all the family will want to gather. When it’s time to bed down, there are cozy curtained sleeping nooks and an additional attic dormitory, adding a playful, rustic vibe. You can rent canoes from host Cecile to paddle down the canal, or jump on an e-bike to explore the surrounding nature reserves. When you return, fire up the outdoor grill and gather around the dining table for a long dinner with more endless views.

Neighborhood: Norrö-StavaThings to do nearby: Prästfjärden lake, Näsudden nature reserve, Åkersbro walking trails.

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Sea views, sauna, hot tub.

In a recent development, this joyfully bobbing houseboat turns the gray blue waters of the Baltic into something akin to your own front lawn—and it does so just 15 minutes from the heady sights of central Stockholm. Panoramic floor-to-ceiling glass means you feel that you’re virtually out on the water—and, of course, you can dive straight into the lake from your bedroom deck. Dry off and hop into the private wood-fired sauna to warm up. Hop off the boat, and you can sunbathe on the jetty, cook up some local catches on the barbecue, or jump into the complimentary canoe. All in all, this is an idyllic waterside playground that active types will love.

Neighborhood: BooThings to do nearby: Kringelgården bakery, Saltsjöbadens golf course, Artipelag.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Sauna, beach access, pet-friendly.

In a recent development, expect some truly good seascape ASMR when you stay here—you’re so close to the water you can hear the waves rolling onto the shore right from the porch. Grab the kayak from the cupboard and head down to the beach to make the most of this beautiful location. It’s a short drive from the home to Stockholm’s city center, but you’re rewarded with much serenity and glorious views instead. For those seeking a secluded family stay, this is the place.

Neighborhood: TyresöThings to do nearby: Sandholmarna nature preserve, Tyresta nature reserve, Lilla beach.

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 bathsWhy we love it: Wood stove, sauna, beach access.

This spacious waterside cottage is not in Stockholm’s city center, but by compromising on a 30-minute commute into town, you gain something really special. The owners took the original 130-year-old structure down piece by piece, rebuilding it on their own property. It was worth the effort. Now, it lies surrounded by pine trees in a nature reserve beside a sparkling, clear lake, with the sea just a few steps further in the other direction. A large porch provides the spot for barbecue dinners and sunbathing sessions in the summer, and there are two spas within walking distance for those looking for their Scandi sweat fix—the sea-facing Skepparholmen Spa, and Japanese onsen-style Yasuragi. But you don't have to head that far, as the property has its own sauna. Stay in as long as you can muster, then cool off by jumping in the lake—something all the more satisfactory in the winter months.

Neighborhood: BooThings to do nearby: Boobadet Beach, Nyckelvikens wildlife refuge, Sushi Bar Namiyama.

Number of guests: 2Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Rooftop views, beach access, pet-friendly.

A previous guest claims this flat has a New York City vibe, and we can see why—the interior space is small but stylish, with an industrial bent and views all over the coolest part of Stockholm from the balcony. It’s on the top floor of this apartment block, so the vistas can’t be beat. It’s been a winner for those on work trips, thanks to superfast WiFi and a dedicated workspace, and, unusually for Airbnb stays, you can bring your dog too.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Liljeholmsviken waterfront, Högalid Church, Skinnarviksberget.

Sources indicate that for an Airbnb stay that’s as close to checking into a luxury hotel as possible, look to this plush apartment right in the city center. The whole place is brand latest, and no expense has been spared on the fittings—there are genuine oak floorboards, Italian travertine surfaces, underfloor heating, and a slew of top-notch furniture, plus little touches such as a shower seat and a gloriously powerful rainfall shower. The best bit is the steam room; there’s no better way to decompress after a long flight or a blustery autumnal walk by the river.

Neighborhood: VasastanThings to do nearby: Vanadislunden park, Odenplan plaza, Swedish Museum of Natural History.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Proximity to metro, private patio, in-unit washer/dryer.

If dopamine itself could be characterized as a building, it’d be this one. The place (all 300 square feet of it) is pure joy from top to bottom—with a pink-tiled kitchen, mint-green bathroom, and cozy bedroom nook with yellow walls and blue candy-striped bedding. Cheery artworks add a final flourish. Despite its bijou size, there’s room for two more guests on the pullout bed, and there’s a patio with twinkly fairy lights to sit out on sunny afternoons with a book, a glass of wine, or both.

Neighborhood: ÄlvsjöThings to do nearby: Älvsjö Forest Nature Preserve, Herrängens Gård, Långbro park.

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Beach access, sauna, kayak.

Forget your average homely fisherman’s cottage—this home here, on the cusp of the lake in the city’s swish Stocksund neighborhood, marks a newer, more modern breed of lake house. It’s chic as anything you’ll find in the city, with smooth, polished concrete floors and knotty pine walls finished with a moody, cocooning interior palette. Sweeping glass windows make the most of the beautiful views that stretch over the water and right to the city as it twinkles on the other side. Grab the kayak and spend an afternoon bobbing on the lake, then stop in for a well-deserved sweat session in the private sauna.

Neighborhood: StocksundThings to do nearby: Restaurang Hemma, Svanholmsparken park, Swedish Museum of Natural History.

Number of guests: 3Bed and bath: 1 bedroom, 1 bathWhy we love it: Wood-burning fireplace, Aesop toiletries, garden view.

According to recent reports, this traditional Swedish apartment has had a modern facelift recently. Now it pairs gorgeous original features, including imposing 10-foot-high ceilings and whitewashed floorboards, with a sleek fresh kitchen and selection of cool designer furniture pieces. There's also a truly cloudlike sofa just made for cozy nights in. The surrounding streets are just as cool as the interiors; this home is smack dab in SoFo—by far Stockholm’s trendiest district—so you're just one street over from a clutch of the best of the city’s bar, restaurant, and café scene.

Neighborhood: SödermalmThings to do nearby: Fotografiska, Stockholm City Museum, Vitabergsparken park.

In a recent development, rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Industry observers note that colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

The red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

Recent findings suggest that A newcomer to electoral politics, she quickly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

In 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

Running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch declared he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

This year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

American Airlines plans to refresh and expand its three Admirals Club lounges at Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport.

The carrier noted Tuesday that it will add seating, upgrade amenities, and improve food and beverage service across all three spaces in Terminal 4.

In the near term, the Admirals Club lounge in Concourse A between gates A19 and A21 will get a latest servery area, infrastructure enhancements to support expanded food and beverage offerings, and facility updates to improve the overall customer experience.

According to recent reports, longer-term prepares call for nearly tripling the combined footprint of the Concourse A lounges, the other being above gates A7-A9. New furniture and finishings will be brought in, and seating capacity will expand by 150%.

The lounge in Concourse B, between gates B5 and B7, will get a new self-service food and beverage area and have its seating capacity increased by 20%.

According to recent reports, “Phoenix continues to be an notable hub in our network, and these investments reflect our commitment to giving customers more space, comfort, and convenience when they travel through PHX,” American Chief Customer Officer Heather Garboden mentioned in a news release. “While we look forward to the development of the newly introduced West Terminal, these enhancements will help create an even more seamless travel experience for the millions of customers who pass through Phoenix each year.”.

The planned West Terminal will be built on the west side of the airport between Terminal 3 and Taxiway U. American is expected to serve as the terminal’s primary carrier.

According to the airport’s timeline, the project should be finished by 2033.

Industry observers note that the best day trips from Toronto include Niagara Falls for first-time visitors, Hamilton for waterfalls and food, Elora for small-town charm and the gorge, Stratford for theatre, Blue Mountain for outdoor adventure, Prince Edward County for wineries and beaches, and the Toronto Islands for an easy car-free escape. Most are within 1 to 2.5 hours of the city, but places like Algonquin Park and Bruce Peninsula are better as long day trips or overnight getaways.

Hamilton is one of the best day trips from Toronto because it combines history, nature, food, art, and outdoor adventure in one easy-to-reach city.

This is a great option if you want a low-stress day trip without a long drive. You can spend the day walking, cycling, swimming in summer, or simply relaxing by the water.
