    #88452. Why United Airlines Is The Only US Carrier Left With An Overseas Hub

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1518 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why United Airlines Is The Only US Carrier Left With An Overseas Hub

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1518 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In general, the US legacy carriers primarily operate their networks within the continental US.
    • United currently operates up to 12 daily flights to 15 different destinations in five countries out of Guam Antonio B.
    • It has been revealed that in 1968, Continental Airlines and regional shareholders established Air Micronesia, initially headquartered in the Northern Mariana Islands.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In general, the US legacy carriers primarily operate their networks within the continental US. All of American Airlines' ten hub airports are located within the continental US, as are all of Delta's nine hub airports. United Airlines, however, has seven hub airports in the continental US, as well as a hub in Guam, an overseas territory of the US located thousands of miles away from Washington. It's the only such operation by any US airline, and it carries on the legacy of an operation that goes back nearly 60 years.

    United currently operates up to 12 daily flights to 15 different destinations in five countries out of Guam Antonio B. Won Pat International Airport (GUM). It is the start/end for the carrier's famous 'Island Hopper' service, and the airline also runs direct services from GUM to San Francisco with a stopover in Honolulu. This route uses a Boeing 777-300ER, while the rest of the GUM routes use the Boeing 737. United is by far the largest airline serving Guam, and it also serves as a vital link connecting Guam to the outside world.

    It has been revealed that in 1968, Continental Airlines and regional shareholders established Air Micronesia, initially headquartered in the Northern Mariana Islands. Operating under the callsign 'Air Mike', the airline initially operated Boeing 727s and became a crucial component in the region's economic development during the late 20th century. Air Micronesia held a near monopoly in the market, and its 727s were crucial in connecting what were previously remote islands to the outside world.

    Continental would eventually own 100% of Air Micronesia, rebranding the airline to 'Continental Micronesia' while the headquarters eventually shifted to Guam. While other airlines attempted to connect Guam to the US at certain points and others served Micronesia from foreign countries, Continental Micronesia was by far the largest airline in this market. Among its most famous routes was the 'Island Hopper', connecting Guam to Honolulu with five stopovers, and the airline also had a substantial international network.

    In a recent development, in 1999, Continental Micronesia began transitioning from using the 727 to the 737NG for most operations, and in 2003, the Guam International Airport Facility pushed commuter airlines out of GUM's Commuter Terminal and leased the facility to Continental. The airline would become Guam's largest private-sector employer, while connecting GUM to over 20 destinations.

    In 2010, Continental Airlines revealed that it would merge with United Airlines, keeping the United name. In 2017, Continental Micronesia was formally merged into United Airlines (it had previously operated as a subsidiary of United Continental Holdings), and today, all Guam flights are directly operated by United.

    Sources indicate that airlines are hardly afraid of shutting down unprofitable hubs, and United itself dehubbed the Cleveland hub that it also inherited from Continental during the merger in 2014. However, the Guam operations were making money for the airline, and they're a vital link to the communities served. In addition, United absolutely dominates Guam, and the hub offers a unique strategic position within the carrier's network that couldn't otherwise be replicated by another hub.

    Recent findings suggest that guam itself is a hub for lucrative military and government activity, and United's position in Guam means that it essentially receives all government travel contracts. Because of the airline's dominance in GUM, it can also charge high fares due to the lack of competition. Altogether, Guam is actually one of United's most lucrative hubs, even if it is also one of its smallest. The operation makes the airline money, and so it will remain a United hub, even as other US legacy carriers have dehubbed their hubs outside of the US mainland.

    Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD).

    Los Angeles International Airport (LAX).

    Denver International Airport (DEN).

    Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR).

    Industry observers note that guam Antonio B. Won Pat International Airport (GUM).

    San Francisco International Airport (SFO).

    Houston George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH).

    Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

    Sources indicate that in March 2026, the carrier began transitioning from using the 737-800 to the 737 MAX 8 for its Guam operations, with the switch having been completed in October. These ten aircraft feature a significantly upgraded interior compared to the old 737-800s, and they feature signs in English and Japanese rather than English and Spanish, while the front row of economy can be collapsed to accommodate a stretcher for medevac flights. In addition, two United First seats are blocked on the Island Hopper to be used as a pilot crew rest facility.

    Going into the 2010s, United Airlines and Delta Air Lines both operated hubs at Tokyo Narita International Airport (NRT). These hubs had operated for decades (Delta inherited NRT operations from Northwest Airlines, while United acquired the NRT routes from Pan Am) and essentially connected US passengers to Asia, serving as a central hub. But in the mid-2010s, United gradually discontinued intra-Asia routes out of NRT, and Delta exited NRT entirely in 2020 (it will return in 2027 with a single route from Seattle).

    In a recent development, whereas United's Guam hub primarily serves the local market, the NRT hubs operated by United and Delta mainly existed for connections. However, the arrival of the Boeing 787 and Airbus A350 allowed these airlines to serve more destinations in Asia nonstop from the US, and nonstop flights typically earn a fare premium over one-stop options. As such, the NRT hubs weren't necessary anymore, since they were essentially set up due to range limitations of older widebodies like the Boeing 747-200.

    Recent findings suggest that in addition to the improved economics of newly introduced widebody aircraft, United declared a joint venture with All Nippon Airways in 2011, while Delta announced a joint venture with Korean Air in 2017. With these, the intra-Asia routes are covered by their joint venture partners, eliminating the need to operate these flights with their own metal. In other words, United's NRT hub has been replaced by nonstop flights to Asia and ANA's operations out of Tokyo, while Delta's NRT hub has been replaced by Korean Air's hub in Seoul.

    Apart from the carrier's one-stop flight from GUM to San Francisco via Honolulu with the 777-300ER, all of United's Guam routes now use the 737 MAX 8. There are right now ten of them stationed in GUM, and they operate to Taipei, Manila, Airai, Saipan, Yap, Pohnpei, Chuuk, Tokyo Narita, Tokyo Haneda, Osaka, and Nagoya. In addition, the airline's flight to Airai continues to Manila on some days of the week, while the flight to Chuuk is part of the Island Hopper, flying from Guam to Honolulu via Chuuk, Pohnpei, Kosrae, Kwajalein, and Majuro.

    Several of these routes do not operate daily, as local demand is ultimately limited and the 737 MAX 8 is a relatively large aircraft, able to carry up to 166 passengers in United's configuration. Japan is United's largest market out of GUM, as it connects the airport to four airports in Japan while operating up to five daily flights between GUM and Japan. Notably, United does not serve Nagoya from the mainland US nonstop.

    Recent findings suggest that some of these routes can be extremely long, which makes the fuel savings of the 737 MAX 8 over the 737-800 highly impactful. Meanwhile, the 777-300ER is flown to Guam almost entirely due to strong demand for cargo, as this is the aircraft in United's fleet with the highest cargo capacity. The airline only has 22 of these planes, which make up less than 10% of its overall widebody fleet, and yet the cargo revenue is strong enough to justify its use on the San Francisco-Honolulu-Guam route.

    While United's Guam operations have generally been successful, the hub has been facing difficulties in recent years due to the COVID-19 pandemic as well as a decline in demand from Japan, the largest market for the hub. Ordinarily, United may simply shift capacity to another hub, but that isn't easy to do with Guam. The airport is thousands of miles away from any of United's other hubs, the carrier has a pilot and flight attendant base in Guam, and the ten 737s are specially configured for these services.

    Recent findings suggest that what United has done with these assets is move them back to NRT. In recent years, the carrier has introduced newly introduced fifth freedom routes from NRT to Cebu, Kaohsiung, and Ulaanbaatar, using the flight numbers of the carrier's nonstop flights to NRT from the mainland US and operating the flights with Guam-based 737s. Crucially, these destinations are not served by ANA, which means that United is expanding the joint venture's Asia coverage while deploying assets that would have otherwise been underutilized.

    Industry observers note that it's one of the most creative ways to utilize assets when the standard operation is no longer producing the returns that it once did. Not only that, but the airline has generated tremendous excitement and publicity over these routes, with the Ulaanbaatar route standing out in particular, and this is beneficial for loyalty program and credit card sign-ups, which is where the carrier makes its real money.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    A judge mentioned he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

    Industry observers note that judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

    “This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg mentioned.

    The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

    Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

    Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”.

    The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

    “You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

    Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump mentioned last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

    Separately, Boasberg noted he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

    Industry observers note that the administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

    For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

    #88448. Finnair Celebrates International Men’s Day With All-Male Crew On Flight

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (955 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Finnair Celebrates International Men’s Day With All-Male Crew On Flight

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There’s still quite a gender gap in the airline industry, with a disproportionate number of pilots being male, and a disproportionate number of flight attendants being female.
    • Recent findings suggest that today is (apparently) International Men’s Day.
    • In a recent development, the crew consisted of 10 people, comprised of two pilots and eight flight attendants.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There’s still quite a gender gap in the airline industry, with a disproportionate number of pilots being male, and a disproportionate number of flight attendants being female. Airlines will sometimes have special celebrations with all-female crews, so here’s an interesting twist on that.

    Recent findings suggest that today is (apparently) International Men’s Day. We often see airlines commemorate International Women’s Day, but there aren’t many airlines that celebrate the equivalent for men… well, except Finnair! The airline has today operated its annual flight with an all-male crew. This was the case for Finnair flight AY1331, from Helsinki (HEL) to London (LHR), using an Airbus A350-900.

    In a recent development, the crew consisted of 10 people, comprised of two pilots and eight flight attendants. The gate agents were also all men. So, why is this key? Finnair highlights how only around 10% of cabin crew at the airline are male, but the organization hopes to see that number grow in the future.

    I think this is a fun concept, and it would be nice to see a closer to 50/50 gender ratio in both the cockpit and cabin, as it would show that everyone is given a fair chance at such a career.

    I think it’s worth acknowledging that at many airlines, hiring of flight attendants is still primarily or exclusively based on gender. Now, the policies do vary significantly by airline, but perhaps an extreme example is India’s largest airline, IndiGo, which only hires female flight attendants. It’s literally written on the application, that it’s a job for “Female Indian nationals.”.

    It’s all so strange, because the airline has this super enthusiastic page about the importance of diversity in the workplace, and notes “all employment decisions are made solely on the basis of merit and qualifications, without regard to a candidate’s gender…” You mean except the single largest portion of your workforce, which is cabin crew?

    What’s interesting is that while those gender restrictions exist in the cabin, roughly 18% of the carrier’s pilots are female, which is way above the global average of 7%. That’s obviously a conscious effort, so I guess the idea is that women can become pilots but men can’t become flight attendants.

    In fairness, I suspect part of the motivation here is that IndiGo flight attendants share hotel rooms on layovers, and that is a bit more complicated with mixed genders. Then again, it seems easy enough to just try to pair male flight attendants on trips, so it’s hardly a hurdle that can’t be overcome.

    While we’re used to seeing airlines celebrate International Women’s Day, it’s rare to see an airline celebrating International Men’s Day. Finnair has operated an all-male flight today, intended to highlight how only 10% of flight attendants at the airline are male, and the airline wants to change that. While an unconventional initiative nowadays, I think this is still pretty cool.

    • Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)….
    • With banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail.
    • We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Dad, here’s a blog post you should pay attention to (and thanks to Steve for flagging this)….

    With banks, it’s typically possible to get your account statements by email or mail. There’s no denying that consumer preferences have shifted over the years, and along those lines, Amex has just sent an email to card members, informing them that “we’re making the switch to paperless.” Here’s the main part of the email:.

    We’re making the switch to paperless billing statements and account communications, beginning February 2027.

    Here’s what happens nextWe want to help you get ready to make the switch too. So, we’ve enrolled your account listed above in the paperless delivery option – but for now, we’ll continue to send you communications about your account in the mail. We’ll also mail your billing statements for the closing dates of November 2026, December 2026, and January 2027.

    According to recent reports, after that, we’ll send account communications to you by email, and you’ll receive your monthly billing statements electronically. When they’re ready, you’ll be able to view them anytime by logging in to your account online at americanexpress.com or in the American Express App.

    It has been revealed that now, that makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, but I don’t believe that’s actually the case? Because further down in the email, it notes this:.

    In a recent development, not ready to go paperless? No problem! You can re-enroll in paper billing statements and account communications by going to americanexpress.com/paperlesssettings, selecting “U.S. Mail,” and following the prompts to opt back in.

    So it seems like what’s happening here is that Amex will try to force everyone into paperless billing by making it the default, but maybe those who specifically once again state their preferences for paper billing will be able to maintain that communication method?

    Suffice it to say that going back 25 years, a vast majority of people got paper statements for their credit cards, while nowadays a vast majority of people get paperless statements, obviously reflecting the shift we’ve seen in how the internet is used.

    According to recent reports, it’s funny, because I’m sure 99% of OMAAT readers would be confused at the thought of getting paper bills, and would wonder what purpose that serves. But then there are also people like my dad, who rely on paper statements for their credit cards, pay their statement by phone, etc.

    So it does sound like people will have the option of opting back into paper billing after being auto-enrolled in paperless billing, so the concept isn’t being eliminated altogether. Still, for my dad, there would likely be quite the learning curve.

    Sources indicate that then again, up until less than a decade ago he didn’t have a cell phone and insisted he didn’t need one, while now he kind of loves it, for everything from texting, to Googling all kinds of stuff. That’s of course a double-edged sword as well, because he seems to believe that if the Google AI summary states something, it must be true. We’re not talking things like vaccines. Instead, we’re talking things like whether the salmon at Red Lobster is good, etc. Anyway, I digress….

    As of February 2027, Amex will be automatically moving those with paper billing to paperless billing. While the message makes it sound like people will be forced to switch to paperless billing, that doesn’t seem to be the case, as Amex is also telling people they can once again enroll in paper billing statements and account communications if they’re “not ready to go paperless.” So Amex just seems to be trying to thin the ranks here of those using this feature.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s.
    • To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet at the moment consists of 25 planes, including:.
    • Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was revealed by the manufacturer’s CEO at this week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-latest business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

    To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet at the moment consists of 25 planes, including:.

    Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was revealed by the manufacturer’s CEO at this week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

    According to recent reports, the strategy is for the 787-9s to get all-latest cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats at the moment on the planes).

    The 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the first of these Dreamliners will be retrofitted in the next 18 to 24 months (so hopefully by some point in 2028), and then it’ll likely take a couple of years for the fleet to be upgraded.

    We’ll talk more about the upcoming business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

    The plane will also have up to 70% more premium seats than before. Currently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

    It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

    Aeromexico’s latest premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

    Seth Miller from PaxEx.Aero flags how Aeromexico’s latest Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new product. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

    Recent findings suggest that aeromexico CEO Dr. Andres Conesa unveiled the carrier's new premium economy cabin plus refreshed business class seat at #APEXFTEExpo in Singapore this week.Full teaser video in the story: paxex.aero/first-look-a….#PaxEx$RTX.

    I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

    It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the new Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

    I imagine that we’ll learn more in the coming months, as this was an unusual way to unveil a latest product. But this does seem to be officially happening, so it’s something to look forward to… down the road.

    Aeromexico is planning some massive upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-new cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

    As this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these new cabins to roll out starting at some point in 2028, so some patience will be required. I can’t wait to learn more!

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Avelo Airlines' network for the winter 2026/27 season looks rather different to how it did in 2025/26.
    • On the international side, scheduling data from Cirium, an aviation analytics firm, indicates that all of the cuts impact short-haul services to key leisure markets in Mexico and the Caribbean.
    • Wilmington International Airport (ILM) in North Carolina is a common factor when examining Avelo's winter network versus 12 months ago.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Avelo Airlines' network for the winter 2026/27 season looks rather different to how it did in 2025/26. Most notably, 31 of the routes the carrier served this time last year are not being operated this time around, with 25 domestic and six international. Of the domestic cuts, a third are concentrated at one airport, highlighting the brutally competitive nature of the airline industry in the States.

    On the international side, scheduling data from Cirium, an aviation analytics firm, indicates that all of the cuts impact short-haul services to key leisure markets in Mexico and the Caribbean. While the last year has seen Avelo make various route cuts, the airline is in flux, and it has a lot to look forward to fleet-wise with the Embraer E2 set to modernize its ops. The airline has ordered 50, with deliveries from 2028.

    Wilmington International Airport (ILM) in North Carolina is a common factor when examining Avelo's winter network versus 12 months ago. Overall, the facility has lost winter service to nine destinations, four of which are in Florida: Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL), Southwest Florida International Airport (RSW), Orlando International Airport (MCO), and West Palm Beach.

    Avelo Airlines' Current Operating Bases.

    The remaining five route cuts concerned services from Wilmington to destinations in the northeast of the US. These included major hubs such as Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD), as well as smaller destinations such as Islip, Manchester, and Rochester.

    Avelo commented on its presence in Wilmington in a statement obtained earlier this year by Wilmington Biz.

    "Wilmington is also not a protected airport. Most of the affected routes cannot handle more than one airline serving them due to demand.".

    While Wilmington has been the hardest-hit airport by Avelo's winter cuts, it is far from the only US facility to have lost routes. Elsewhere in North Carolina, the carrier is no longer serving five destinations from Raleigh-Durham International (RDU) that it did this time last year: these are Albany, Fort Myers, Grand Rapids, Manchester, and Rochester. Of course, the cuts extend beyond North Carolina.

    For instance, Tweed New Haven Airport (HVN) has lost three winter Avelo Airlines routes: William P. Hobby Airport (HOU), Louis Armstrong International Airport (MSY), and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD). Wilmington in Delaware (ILG) saw three cuts, namely to Jacksonville (JAX), Nashville (BNA), and Raleigh-Durham, while Nashville itself lost Rochester.

    Returning to the state of North Carolina, Concord-Padgett Regional Airport (USA) no longer handles winter Avelo Airlines flights to West Palm Beach. Elsewhere, the American ultra-low-cost carrier also no longer flies from Islip to Lakeland Linder International Airport (LAL) in Florida in the winter. Still, it remains relatively busy, with 1,616 flights scheduled to operate this November. These will offer 300,784 seats.

    On the international side, Wilmington International Airport has also lost winter Avelo Airlines flights to Punta Cana International Airport (PUJ) in the Dominican Republic. The carrier has also ceased its winter services to this popular Caribbean leisure destination from Bradley International Airport (BDL) in Windsor Locks, Connecticut, and Raleigh-Durham International Airport (RDU).

    Sources indicate that windsor Locks has also lost winter Avelo Airlines flights to Cancún International Airport (CUN) in Mexico, and the carrier has ceased winter service from both Windsor Locks and Raleigh-Durham to Sangster International Airport (MBJ) in Montego Bay, Jamaica. The cessation of these routes marked the end of Avelo Airlines' international flights, which had only commenced operations back in 2024.

    • 31 and remain with the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027, CEO Robert Isom unveiled Friday.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines is making another change to its senior leadership team, with Chief Operating Officer David Seymour set to retire at the end of the year.

    Seymour will step down on Dec. 31 and remain with the Fort Worth, Texas-based carrier in an advisory capacity through the first quarter of 2027, CEO Robert Isom unveiled Friday.

    Seymour has served as American’s chief operating officer since 2020. He joined the airline in 1999 and held various leadership positions overseeing technical operations, crew scheduling, and flight operations.

    “He’s the guy you want in the room when the stakes are high,” Isom wrote in a letter to employees.

    It has been revealed that jonCarlo “JC” Gulbranson, American’s current senior vice president of operations, will succeed Seymour on Jan. 1. He will report directly to Isom and assume oversight of the carrier’s technical operations, safety, and regulatory compliance teams.

    Gulbranson began his airline career at Northwest Airlines in 2000 before joining US Airways in 2008. He helped oversee the integration of flight operations systems following the merger with American.

    It has been revealed that american will also move its corporate security team under its government affairs division. A fresh reporting structure for the airline’s regional operations will be revealed in December.

    “For nearly three decades, jet fuel hasn’t just been in my veins. It’s been part of my DNA. To this day, I wake up excited to get to work — which is just about all you can ask for in a job,” Seymour wrote in a LinkedIn post.

    The changes follow a broader management reshuffle announced in August as the carrier works to narrow its profitability gap with competitors Delta and United.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard.
    • This system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service complications at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge.
    • According to recent reports, emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Emirates is known for its incredibly high service standards, and that’s largely thanks to the hierarchical system onboard. You have different ranks of flight attendants, then you have supervisors overseeing business class and economy, and then those supervisors report to the purser.

    This system ensures that there’s accountability onboard, and I think that lack of hierarchy is one of the reasons we have service complications at airlines in the US, as no one is really in charge. Anyway, along those lines, Emirates has just introduced a latest initiative, which will no doubt be controversial among flight attendants….

    According to recent reports, emirates has a rank above pursers, which are the Standard Pursers (which is a weird name, but the idea is that they’re there to audit and enforce “standards”). These are specially trained former pursers who no longer work flights in a standard capacity (at least until now), but instead, they audit the crews onboard flights. They have completely different uniforms.

    Emirates’ Chief Operations Officer, Adel Alredha, has just taken to Instagram to highlight a latest initiative involving this small group of employees:.

    On 3 November, Emirates introduced a newly introduced initiative on select flights, which will have Standard Pursers work alongside cabin crew teams to provide support and guidance to ensure consistently high standards of service.

    This step reflects the airline’s ongoing commitment to maintaining service quality and elevating the customer experience.

    So rather than just auditing the cabins, these Emirates employees will actually be working in the cabin, and that’s sure to ruffle some feathers….

    A post shared by Adel Alredha (@adelalredha).

    Emirates is of course an incredibly global airline with staff from around the world, and I know a thing or two about the internal politics that crews deal with, the different working environments based on who is purser, etc.

    For example, you have some pursers who are incredibly strict to the point that they make their colleagues feel uncomfortable and nervous, while you have other pursers who try to encourage good service by creating a fun environment, etc.

    According to recent reports, it goes without saying that historically when a flight had an auditor onboard, everyone would be on their absolute best behavior. In a way that’s no doubt a bit chaotic and stressful, since they’re worried about repercussions if something goes wrong.

    When it comes to this initiative, on the one hand, it’s probably good for these auditors to get some renewed firsthand experience with service, guest expectations, etc. On the other hand, I have to imagine that from the perspective of other crew members, this won’t necessarily be perceived as an effort to “provide support and guidance.”.

    As one commenter on the Instagram post notes, “this is like sending a child to school along with mama with a stick to correct the kid every step.” Another commenter notes “as if there wasn’t already enough pressure on the crew.”.

    In a recent development, I am curious if these flights are still staffed with a regular purser in addition to this special rank of purser, because that could also cause a bit of a butting-of-heads. If an auditor is onboard in their official capacity, it’s clear what everyone’s role onboard is (everyone is there to make sure they perform well!). But if the auditor is there to simply “provide support,” that blurs the lines a little bit, no?

    Anyway, there aren’t actually that many of these auditor pursers at the airline, so presumably only a small percentage of flights will have them. But if you do notice a crew member with a completely different uniform (more silver in color), now you know what’s going on. That would also be a great person to provide any feedback to, because they actually have the ability to get those details to the right person.

    Emirates has Standard Pursers, who are essentially auditors who are assigned select flights, in order to evaluate service from the crew. As of this month, these auditors are also starting to work on flights alongside the crew, to “provide support and guidance.”.

    There’s no denying that this is an initiative that will make some crew members nervous, since this definitely blurs the line of auditing vs. having an extra set of helping hands. However, given the relatively small number of auditors, they shouldn’t be on too many flights. But if you do see someone in a completely different uniform (other than the standard female purser uniform), then now you know what’s going on.

    What do you make of this Emirates initiative?

    Industry observers note that I am a predominantly ground based cabin crew manager for a large European airline but also work as supernumerary crew on 2-3 long haul flights per year. On those flights I wear a uniform and am additional to the crew complement and my role is to support and to a lesser degree assess member of my flying team. I find it really beneficial as airline crew are typically remote workers and rarely have access to their ground manager. It also gives me the ability to see first hand lots of the pain points my team complain to me about - service routines, galley layouts etc. I don't think these kind of roles are that unusual in the airline world.     #88439. Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1221 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Zinke PAC gave to family foundation he was investigated for

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1221 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025.
    • Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.
    • The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that rep. Ryan Zinke, R-Mont., leaves a meeting of the House Republican Conference at the Capitol Hill Club on July 15, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Outgoing Montana GOP Rep. Ryan Zinke gave $200,000 in campaign cash to a family foundation headed by his wife that was once at the center of a federal investigation and an ethics scandal that led him to resign as Interior secretary in 2019.

    The gift, which has not previously been reported, was made on Aug. 31 from Zinke’s leadership political action committee to the nonprofit Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation, campaign finance records show. The donation is more than the foundation has reported receiving in any year since it was founded nearly two decades ago.

    Zinke’s wife, son, and sister presently serve on its board of directors, according to the foundation’s annual filing with the state of Montana.

    According to recent reports, in a brief interview, Zinke denied that any portion of the money transferred to the foundation will directly benefit him or any of his family members who sit on the board of directors. “No, no, never," he said when asked if any family members will draw a salary from the gift.

    The money will instead go to building a storage barn and kid’s sledding park on the property controlled by the foundation, Zinke mentioned.

    None of the records indicate Zinke violated the law or directly benefited from the gift to his foundation.

    “While it's not uncommon for a politician to transfer leftover money from a political war chest to charity, it is pretty rare for a politician to transfer leftover political funds to a charity that they or a relative controls,” stated Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at Glitch One, a bipartisan group that seeks to reduce influence of money in politics.

    Instead, outgoing members typically transfer remaining campaign cash to local party committees or candidates, Beckel added.

    Ethics experts say Zinke’s move highlights ongoing concerns over the broad latitude campaign finance law gives leadership PACs in how they spend money.

    “I definitely think it is something to be concerned about,” noted Stuart McPhail, director of campaign finance litigation at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a nonprofit watchdog.

    “Leadership PACs are really nothing more than personal slush funds under today's rules,” he said, noting that unlike regular campaign committees, member leadership PACs are not prohibited from donating to charities or organizations that could directly benefit the member or relative.

    Zinke, a former Navy SEAL who commanded special forces during the Iraq War, converted his traditional campaign committee to a leadership PAC — Commander Zinke Leadership Fund — in March 2026, shortly after announcing he would not run for reelection. It last reported having $1.4 million cash on hand in October of this year.

    Recent findings suggest that it marks the second time one of Zinke’s political committees made a payment to the organization. In 2019, the committee Zinke ran during his earlier years in Congress — he served one term in the House before being tapped as Trump’s first-term Interior secretary — gave over $11,000 to the foundation before winding down operations.

    The Great Northern Veterans Peace Foundation was founded by Zinke and his wife in 2007 in his hometown of Whitefish, Mont., with plans to provide winter recreational activities for children. Its latest tax filing reports revenue of $15,000 and roughly equal expenses in 2024 for snow plowing and park maintenance.

    Zinke’s dealings with the organization were the subject of an ongoing inspector general investigation when he resigned as Interior secretary in January 2019.

    Investigators ultimately did not find that Zinke violated conflict-of-interest laws, but they concluded that he failed to comply with federal ethics obligations and “misused his official position in violation of federal regulations.” The Justice Department declined to prosecute Zinke.

    Zinke stepped down from the foundation in 2017, shortly after his Senate confirmation. But investigators found that he continued to represent the organization in negotiations with the developers of a commercial project adjacent to the foundation’s land and lied to an ethics agent about his involvement in the project.

    The project’s investors included David Lesar, then-chairman of oil services company Halliburton.

    Another Zinke-tied leadership PAC has previously raised eyebrows in Washington.

    Supporting Electing American Leaders PAC — known as SEAL PAC — where Zinke serves as chairman, has been marred by accusations that it funneled money to political consultants instead of candidates. A 2022 CQ Roll Call analysis found that 87 percent of the PAC’s spending went to operating expenses.

    The PAC also made recurring monthly payments to a company registered to Zinke’s son, Wolfgang Zinke, and based at a Zinke family-owned home in Whitefish.

    SEAL PAC’s executive director, Rob Catron, maintained that the payments constitute a consulting fee to Wolfgang Zinke for management of the PAC website, among other tasks. “He earns every penny of it,” Catron said.

    Since May 2022, the PAC has given roughly $270,000 to Wolfgang Zinke’s manufacturer, FG Solutions, for mailing and printing, records show — more than any individual candidate or committee supported by the PAC. The company also received $5,000 from a related super PAC, SEAL PAC USA, which can solicit unlimited contributions for independent expenditures but can’t donate directly to candidates.

    Montana corporate records show Wolfgang Zinke founded FG Solutions – which says it provides services including “personal assistant and any lawful purpose” – just 10 days before it received its first payment from the PAC in 2022.

    Catron defended how the PAC spends money on veterans running for the House, arguing that it takes money to raise money.

    “We raise a lion’s share of our funding through national direct mail fundraising, which is very expensive to do,” he remarked, citing the PAC’s use of a national text message fundraising campaign as a major expense.

    Sources indicate that SEAL PAC raised about $9.6 million this election cycle, distributing about $1.1 million to GOP lawmakers and candidates, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Most of the committee's funds went to operating expenses, including over $3 million paid to Direct Support Services, a Washington-based vendor, for direct mail postage.

    Zinke’s not the only lawmaker to face scrutiny over how they spent surplus campaign cash in recent years.

    In 2023, Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., set off alarm bells for transferring $200,000 from his campaign committee to The Sanders Institute, a nonprofit founded by his wife and stepson, following a $350,000 donation from his 2020 presidential campaign coffers.

    The organization briefly shut down during Sanders’ presidential run in 2019 to avoid the appearance of impropriety.

    Sanders’ stepson, David Driscoll — a former executive at Nike and snowboard manufacturer Burton — is listed on the think tank’s website as its executive director, drawing a six-figure annual salary according to tax filings.

    It’s unusual, though not unheard of, for campaign committees to pay family members of the candidate for bona fide work.

    “If [Wolfgang Zinke] is actually performing this work, he’s qualified to do it, and this is his typical market rate for this kind of contract, then it would be permissible, even if this was a campaign account,” McPhail said about SEAL PAC's payments.

    But the payments could present a legal “gray area” over whether personal-use restrictions apply to certain PACs, according to McPhail.

    Recent findings suggest that on the first day of each month, you earn double those rewards on these cards, and earn up to 1,000 bonus points each month. It could be worth strategically making some purchases on the first day of each month to maximize this as much as possible.

    For example, with double points, the Bilt Palladium Card offers 4x points on everyday spending on the first day of the month, so that’s pretty awesome (up to a cap of $500 worth of spending, since that would earn you 1,000 bonus points).

    The status is matched for a period of three months, with no additional activity required to maintain it for that period. Then, during those three months, members can extend the status through January 31, 2028, by completing the following requirements:.

The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

    In a recent development, have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

    Iberia’s standard livery combines a predominantly white fuselage with a red-and-yellow tail inspired by the colors of Spain’s national flag. Introduced in 2013, the design marked the carrier’s first major rebranding in more than three decades.

    According to recent reports, the airline unveiled its latest corporate identity on October 15, 2013, as part of a broader restructuring effort. The redesign replaced the familiar red, orange, and yellow stripes that had appeared on Iberia aircraft since the late 1970s.

    According to recent reports, the most prominent change came on the vertical stabilizer. Iberia introduced a sweeping red-and-yellow design that extends from the tail onto the rear fuselage. A white diagonal section separates the two colors, giving the aircraft a different appearance from the geometric logo used on the previous livery.

    The fuselage also received a substantial update. Large red “IBERIA” titles replaced the smaller lettering used on earlier aircraft, while the horizontal stripes running along the windows were eliminated. The result was a predominantly white aircraft with most of its color concentrated toward the tail.

    Iberia’s latest branding retained the red and yellow of the Spanish flag but removed the royal crown from its main corporate logo. The crown had been part of the airline’s previous identity and remained represented separately on aircraft near their registration markings.

    Sources indicate that the redesign followed Iberia’s 2011 merger with British Airways under International Airlines Group. At the time, the Spanish carrier was undergoing a significant restructuring that included changes to its fleet, route network, and passenger experience.

    It has been revealed that the first aircraft to receive the updated livery was an Airbus A330-300 named *Juan Carlos I*, which was presented in November 2013. The new appearance was subsequently introduced across the airline’s fleet as aircraft underwent scheduled repainting.

    In a recent development, iberia’s earlier livery had been introduced in 1977 and featured a stylized red-and-yellow “IB” logo on the tail. Although the design received minor updates over the years, its basic appearance remained recognizable on aircraft ranging from Boeing 727s and 747s to Airbus A320s and A340s.

    In a recent development, the current scheme has since appeared on several generations of Iberia aircraft, including Airbus A320-family jets, A330s and A350s. It also appears on the airline’s Airbus A321XLR fleet, which entered service in 2024 as Iberia became the launch operator of the long-range narrowbody.

    It has been revealed that iberia has occasionally introduced special liveries celebrating milestones in its history, including retro designs commemorating the airline’s earlier aircraft. Its standard scheme, however, has remained largely unchanged since the 2013 rebranding.

    It has been revealed that looking for a newly introduced airplane model? Head over to our friends at the Midwest Model Store for a wide selection of airlines and liveries.

    #88435. The Airlines Set To Replace Their Boeing 777s With New 777-9s Throughout The 2030s

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1708 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    The Airlines Set To Replace Their Boeing 777s With New 777-9s Throughout The 2030s

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Boeing has roughly 620 orders for an aircraft that has not delivered a single one yet, and some of the very first examples built may never reach the airline that paid for them.
    • So who is really lining up to replace their Boeing 777s with the new 777-9, what exactly are they replacing, and when will passengers see the first one?
    • In a recent development, the scale of the commitment is hard to ignore.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Boeing has roughly 620 orders for an aircraft that has not delivered a single one yet, and some of the very first examples built may never reach the airline that paid for them. The 777-9 is meant to be the jet that carries the world's biggest long-haul airlines through the 2030s, but the program is about seven years behind its original 2020 service date, and the biggest customer has already turned away its first batch. For an industry that aims fleets decades ahead, that is a very awkward way to start a new era.

    So who is really lining up to replace their Boeing 777s with the new 777-9, what exactly are they replacing, and when will passengers see the first one? The answers involve Emirates, Qatar Airways, Cathay Pacific, Singapore Airlines, and Lufthansa, plus a rival Airbus that has already started delivering.

    In a recent development, the scale of the commitment is hard to ignore. According to an order book compiled by Airways Magazine at the end of May 2026, the 777X program stood at 619 orders: 521 777-9s, 63 777-8 freighters, and 35 passenger 777-8s, all of them for Emirates. That is a remarkable number for an aircraft that has not carried a single paying passenger, and it makes the 777X Boeing's most important widebody bet of the decade. Airways also noted that the problem is certification, not demand, which is a rare thing to say about a program this delayed.

    Emirates dominates the list. As reported by Emirates itself, its November 2025 Dubai Airshow deal added 65 more 777-9s, worth $38 billion at list prices, and lifted its total to 270 777Xs. The airline also holds options to convert part of that order into the 777-8 or the proposed, larger 777-10. Airways lists the split as 235 777-9s and 35 777-8s, so the exact mix is still fluid. Qatar Airways is second with 124 aircraft, made up of 90 777-9s and 34 777-8 freighters, followed by Cathay Pacific with 35 and Singapore Airlines with 31.

    British Airways and its parent IAG have 24, Lufthansa Group has 27 (20 passenger jets and seven freighters), Korean Air has 20, and ANA has 20, including two freighters. Air India, Etihad, and Ethiopian Airlines hold 10, 10, and 8. But a long list of customers only tells us who wants the jet. It indicates nothing about what each of them plans to retire in exchange, or how long they will have to keep the old aircraft flying while they wait.

    It has been revealed that for most buyers, the answer is the Boeing 777-300ER, the best-selling long-haul widebody of its generation. Emirates alone flies 119 of them, plus 10 777-200LRs, according to its own fleet table. As noted by Simple Flying, the 777X is also pitched as a successor to high-capacity four-engine jets such as the Boeing 747 and the Airbus A380, which burn far more fuel and cost more to maintain.

    Recent findings suggest that the new jet's biggest selling point is efficiency. According to Simple Flying's analysis of range and capacity, the 777-9 seats around 426 passengers against roughly 396 on a 777-300ER, while keeping a nearly identical range. The GE9X engines are expected to deliver up to 10% better fuel efficiency than the GE90-115B engines on the older jet.

    In a recent development, the wing is the other trick: it spans 235 feet, 5 inches (71.8 meters) in flight, but its tips fold to 212 feet, 9 inches (64.9 meters) on the ground so it still fits standard gates. Boeing's pitch to airlines is simple: keep the long range, burn less fuel, and spend less on maintenance than the aging jets on the ramp.

    It has been revealed that boeing 777-300ER vs. 777-9: the swap in numbers.

    7,370 nautical miles (13,649 km).

    7,285 nautical miles (13,492 km).

    242 feet, 4 inches (73.9 meters).

    251 feet, 9 inches (76.7 meters).

    GE9X (up to 10% better efficiency).

    On paper, that is a clean trade: more seats, similar range, lower fuel burn. The uncomfortable detail is that the older jets have to keep flying while the replacement is late, and that raises a very practical question about timing. Airways Magazine points out that carriers waiting on the 777-9 have had to stretch the lives of older 777-300ERs, A380s, and 747-400s, which adds maintenance, fuel, and cabin-product pressure with every extra year.

    Lufthansa will be the first, with Boeing targeting a 2027 delivery. Emirates stated in November 2025 that it expects its first 777-9 from the second quarter of 2027, and its Boeing deliveries stretch all the way to 2038. That means the airline will be swapping 777-300ERs for 777-9s for more than a decade, which is exactly why this story belongs to the 2030s rather than to next year. Emirates still flies 116 Airbus A380s as well, so the transition will be gradual rather than a clean break.

    In a recent development, others will wait longer. According to Simple Flying, citing the Mainly Miles blog, Singapore Airlines' fleet initiative reveals no 777-9 deliveries in the 12 months to March 31, 2027, with Emirates, Qatar Airways, and Lufthansa ahead in the queue. That timing matters because Singapore Airlines is also planning a newly introduced premium economy product around the aircraft, making the 777-9 part of a future cabin strategy as well as a fleet replacement program.

    In a recent development, even the schedule itself is soft. Airways Magazine reported that FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford signaled the 777X would follow the 737 MAX 7 and MAX 10 into 2027 for certification. So queue position is one thing, but the airlines cannot simply take delivery because they are next in line. The more awkward problem is already sitting on Boeing's property: aircraft built years ago for customers that may no longer want them.

    Between 2019 and 2021, Boeing built around 30 777-9s before the program stalled, including aircraft earmarked for Emirates and Lufthansa, according to German aviation outlet aero.de. By the time they could be delivered, they would be about eight years old and technically behind the final production standard. That creates an unusual problem for a brand-new aircraft: the earliest examples are already old enough to require substantial work before an airline wants them.

    As reported by Simple Flying, Emirates rejected the first batch built for it because bringing those airframes up to the required standard would take extensive and costly rework. Boeing reportedly dismantled one early Emirates-bound 777-9 after the cost to fix it exceeded its value. Lufthansa has since mentioned, on its second-quarter earnings call, that it will refuse some of its earliest aircraft, with Boeing contributing financially to upgrade the rest.

    Qatar Airways has reportedly signaled that it does not want early-build aircraft either, so Boeing may pool the rejected jets and sell them in bundles. According to aero.de, an unnamed US airline is reportedly interested in 20 early 777-9s, which is striking because no major US carrier has ordered the type at all. A discounted early-build 777-9 could therefore find a latest home, but the fact that airlines that ordered the aircraft in the first place are turning some away shows just how unusual this delay has become.

    According to recent reports, according to Simple Flying, Qatar Airways put the A350-1000 into service in February 2018, the 777-9 first flew in January 2020 and still was not certified at Farnborough 2026, and Airbus has already delivered 114 A350-1000s against 367 firm orders. Boeing, meanwhile, has delivered none of its more than 520 777-9s.

    Air Canada is the clearest example. As reported by Business Traveller, the airline ordered eight A350-1000s, with options on eight more, for delivery from the second half of 2030, to modernize a long-haul fleet that includes 19 777-300ERs. Business Traveller calls the A350-1000 a logical replacement for the 777-300ER, and notes it brings a cabin altitude of about 6,000 feet (1,829 meters) versus 8,000 feet (2,438 meters) on the 777 family. No North American airline has ordered the 777-9, so for passengers in the US and Canada, the A350-1000 may arrive first.

    Still, a head start is not the same as a better fit. The 777-9 carries more passengers, and for airlines that fill every seat, that may be the decisive metric. The A350-1000 offers the established nine-abreast cabin and a substantial operating track record, while Boeing's aircraft offers greater capacity and is aimed squarely at airlines that need to move huge numbers of passengers through constrained hubs. That leaves the 777-9 with a clear market, but a narrower one than the raw order total might suggest.

    According to recent reports, the honest answer is volume and density. Emirates and Qatar Airways run some of the busiest trunk routes in the world, and for those carriers, the 777-9's size is a feature rather than a flaw. An A350-1000 cannot match its seat count, and the A380 is out of production, so the 777-9 is effectively the last substantial twin-engine option left for airlines that need capacity above all else. That is the strongest argument Boeing has, and it is also why the aircraft is best suited to a relatively small group of mega-hub operators.

    The test comes in the next 18 months. If Lufthansa takes its first jet in 2027 and Emirates follows soon after, the long order book will start to look like a steady delivery stream. If certification slips again, as Airways Magazine warns could compress the entire handover and training timeline, more carriers may do what Air Canada did and look at the A350-1000 instead. The early-build jets will be worth watching too: how many Boeing can remarket, and at what price, will reveal just how costly the delay has been.

    According to recent reports, emirates has even signed options to stretch part of its order into the 777-10, a bigger variant Boeing is still studying. That may ultimately be the most revealing sign of all: the airlines that have waited longest for the 777-9 are still thinking about what comes after it. By 2035, the question may no longer be whether the 777-9 replaced the 777-300ER. It may be whether Boeing's biggest twinjet has finally found the narrow but extremely valuable market it was designed for.

    Latest Update: Now hiring: Staff to power Democrats’ probes

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1254 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February.
    • Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the fresh year, making the most of their coming majority.
    • According to recent reports, that means staffing up major committees.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., arrives at the Rayburn Building for a House Judiciary Committee hearing in February. He will be a key player in leading oversight efforts next year — and so will Democratic staff. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Democrats in Congress have promised to hit the ground running with sprawling oversight investigations in the fresh year, making the most of their coming majority.

    According to recent reports, that means staffing up major committees. And for the dozens of attorneys and other aides preparing to take on a belligerent Trump administration that has cast Democratic oversight as potentially criminal, the job will come with extra scrutiny.

    Recent findings suggest that arya Hariharan, former chief oversight counsel to Sen. Richard J. Durbin on the Senate Judiciary Committee and now a partner at Holland & Knight, noted the pressure will be on from day one.

    “Are you prepared to not sleep very much and know that every single thing you do is going to be scrutinized, every footnote, every comma?” Hariharan mentioned.

    Still, the way Hariharan sees it, serving on the Hill is worth it. “I hope they all fall in love with it because it’s a lovely place to work,” she says of staffers headed there for the first time.

    It has been revealed that the work done by attorneys and other staff in oversight probes can quickly become part of constitutional law. When Trump adviser Peter Navarro defied a subpoena from Democrats investigating the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol, it touched off debates about executive privilege and contempt of Congress. Probes of Hunter Biden led to similar court fights.

    Sources indicate that some questions have gone all the way up to the Supreme Court, like in Trump v. Mazars, when the House fought to access Trump’s business records during his first administration in furtherance of toughening up government ethics laws.

    There’s every indication that pressure will continue in the upcoming Congress. James Melendres, a partner at Snell & Wilmer, stated Democrats are poised for aggressive oversight efforts, even if they know it could be tough to make headway against litigation resistant administration officials.

    Sources indicate that “Democrats are going to have less than two years to show results. I think they are going to move really fast,” Melendres said.

    Democrats will likely soon start to send out preservation letters to private companies, institutions and others they intend to probe in the new year, if they haven’t already, Melendres noted.

    “There may be significant pushback from the administration, from agencies and individual government officials who receive requests. I think third-party, nongovernment agencies and individuals are going to be high on the list for these committees,” he noted.

    Industry observers note that in addition to the hiring that happens over the next few weeks, House Democrats will have major decisions to make about chamber and committee rules for the upcoming Congress, including who will hold subpoena authority. And off-Hill observers will be watching closely.

    “For companies, for individuals and their counsel, mapping all of that is going to be a big part of the job between now and early January,” Melendres said.

    Lawmakers need to nail down funding levels for congressional committees and staff — the amount of money involved can make a significant difference in how big investigations get. Major committees, and major investigations, take a large amount of staff and expertise to get going.

    For instance, the special House panel that investigated the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol spent about $14 million in less than 18 months, including for dozens of staffers.

    Recent findings suggest that standing committees, such as Oversight and Judiciary, take a good chunk of change, too. In 2025 the House spent $12.9 million on the House Oversight and Government Reform panel, and $13.1 million on the House Judiciary Committee.

    Those expenditures mean dozens of staff working long hours to review documents, send letters, send subpoenas and conduct interviews. Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is expected to serve as chair next year, said he wouldn’t get into specifics yet about how many resources the new Congress may devote to oversight efforts.

    “But we are talking about the most corrupt administration in the history of the United States, and this is an overwhelming and daunting task that faces us,” Raskin said.

    The Trump administration itself has already signaled it intends to push back forcefully on congressional oversight efforts.

    Earlier this month, President Donald Trump described Democrats’ vows to investigate his administration as “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”.

    Days later, the White House counsel sent a letter saying that subpoena threats from House Oversight ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and others “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.

    Industry observers note that U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz for the Southern District of Texas followed up with letters of his own to Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; and Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., urging them to preserve documents tied to their promised oversight.

    “The American people are entitled to freely associate without their elected officials terrorizing them with aggressive, harassing government action,” Reitz’s letter to Warren noted.

    Members of the incoming majority have signaled they intend to defend themselves and their probes, and Blumenthal said he won’t be deterred by the letter.

    According to recent reports, “There’s no way that I’m going to be intimidated or bullied. It would be laughable and ludicrous, but it is a clear abuse and misuse of prosecutorial powers and weaponization by the Department of Justice,” said Blumenthal, who serves as the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations.

    As for Raskin, he called the White House counsel letter and other missives “absurd on its face.”.

    According to recent reports, “I’m sure they would love to get into a whole series of letters and counter-letters and litigation. They’re trying to distract everybody from the fact that they just lost the worst landslide electoral repudiation in at least a half century in America, and so they’re going to pick a fight,” Raskin told reporters.

    Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the likely incoming speaker, told reporters last week that he intended oversight efforts in his chamber to be led by Raskin and Garcia.

    Recent findings suggest that “We haven’t ruled anything in. We haven’t ruled anything out. We’re going to follow the facts. We’re going to apply the law. We’re going to be guided by the Constitution, and we’re going to let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries said.

    Democrats have already publicly listed a handful of job postings for oversight staff and counsel, ranging from the Science to Armed Services to Judiciary panels, set to start early next year.

    Beyond those hires, House Democrats will have to make one major pick they haven’t yet revealed — the House counsel. The position, first created in the 1970s, is hired by the majority and advocates for the chamber in court. That attorney, along with a group of bipartisan House leaders controlled by the majority, will steer the chamber’s legal strategy.

    According to recent reports, in prior Democratic Congresses, that office has been active in court; Doug Letter frequently argued on behalf of the Democratic House majority seeking to enforce subpoenas on behalf of congressional committees. The position is held by Matthew Berry in the current Republican-controlled House.

    “I mean, I think a lot of people are interested in that job,” Raskin remarked.

    Tech Report: Why Aerolíneas Argentinas Is Basically An Ultra Low Cost Carrier In Disguise

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1466 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.
    • As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.
    • However, I rapidly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This might seem like a rather niche topic to cover in my first week at OMAAT, but after Ben mentioned this story in his intro article, I thought it made sense to follow up fast with an explainer.

    As a flag carrier of the 3rd most populous nation in South America, I went into my Aerolíneas Argentinas flight with them at the start of the year expecting some pretty standard things: enjoying my SkyTeam benefits, lounge access, and, most importantly of all for someone living out of a suitcase, checked bag allowance.

    However, I rapidly discovered that the airline is basically an ultra-low-cost airline masquerading as a full-service carrier.

    I needed to get from Buenos Aires to Mendoza for a friend’s 40th birthday celebrations. Options were pretty limited, with nonstop flights available with either JetSmart or, indeed, Aerolíneas Argentinas. I try to avoid low-cost airlines when possible, because, quite simply, I enjoy the flying experience, and low-cost airlines tend to suck every enjoyable element out of it.

    Other pros to booking Aerolíneas Argentinas, personally:.

    After researching my options, I used Flying Blue miles to book two single tickets from Buenos Aires Jorge Newbery Aeroparque Airport (AEP) to Mendoza’s El Plumerillo Airport (MDZ).

    I can’t remember how much the fares were when I was planning the trip, but each one-way flight cost a total of 7,500 miles and less than $10 in taxes and fees.

    Looking now at example fares for January next year, round-trips for Aerolíneas’ lowest and most restrictive fare category (more on that to come) start at around $120.

    It has been revealed that I know it’s not a hard-and-fast rule, but I’ve come to expect that, most of the time, the baggage allowance listed on the booking confirmation is correct. This is often true with redemptions, such as British Airways, which notably offers and acknowledges a 23 kg baggage allowance when redeeming Avios, even for a short-haul flight in economy.

    The confirmation email I received clearly noted 1x checked bag with a 23 kg limit.

    Again, the attached PDF stated that I’d have 1x checked bag included.

    As the Argentinian scamsters would have it, I learned at check-in that the airline has a 15 kg weight limit for checked bags on domestic flights. I tried to plead my case and highlighted the rather unhelpful check-in agent my booking confirmation, but he basically stated, “that means nothing.”.

    According to recent reports, so they weigh your bag, give you a ticket, and then you have to exit the terminal building and find this little cashier where they collect their scammy little earnings. And what better place to proudly display a “SkyTeam Alliance Member” sign at the very desk where the airline also proudly collects baggage fees from SkyTeam elite status holders, even when traveling on award tickets?

    Once I’d been charged the fee of around $17, I had to join another queue back inside and show them I’d paid for the extra weight before they’d dispatch my bag. You might look at the $32 in fees I paid and think, “What is he complaining about?” But this isn’t about the actual amount of money; it’s the principle.

    Industry observers note that only after the debacle did I learn the extent of Aerolíneas Argentinas’ domestic fare restrictions. Imagine paying $510 (more than four times the cheapest fare) for a “premium economy” ticket and still only getting 15 kg checked baggage allowance, no Fast Pass, no priority boarding (what?), and no lounge access. The latter isn’t such a big deal as Aerolíneas Argentinas doesn’t even have its own lounge at AEP.

    According to recent reports, airline loyalty is really crucial to me, and I generally value it more than the ability to redeem miles. Maybe I’ll get into that another day….

    Things got off to a fairly normal start when I saw the Sky Priority check-in kiosks at Aeroparque.

    In a recent development, that feeling of normalcy lasted as long as it took me to get from the sign to the aforementioned conversation about the checked bag situation at the desk. Despite my very best efforts combining my Castilian Spanish and Geordie charm (we’re called Geordies where I’m from in the North East of England), the man at the check-in desk seemed to take real pleasure in explaining that the checked bag rules on my booking confirmation were irrelevant and I’d have to pay the fee.

    For what it’s worth, Sky Priority check-in was also available at Mendoza.

    Being nickel-and-dimed for a checked bag by a flag carrier airline is shameful.

    Back at Aeroparque, there was no fast track, and the security line was ridiculously long. That remarked, it’s rare in South America to have fast track lanes. For example, no matter whether you’re flying economy or first class (even Air France La Première), everyone waits in the same line to clear pre-departure passport control at São Paulo’s Guarulhos.

    Thanks to my Priority Pass, I did have access to the surprisingly nice AMAE lounge in the national departures part of the airport.

    Industry observers note that even from the outside, my 15-year-old Embraer 190 looked like it had seen better days. The zebra-striped dirt streaks running from each window suggested this place hadn’t been washed or hit the maintenance hangar for a while.

    Inside the Embraer, however, could have been a lot worse. The older seats had thick padding, and despite being a small 2-2-configured cabin, it felt bright and spacious.

    It was the Uber advertising on every single headrest that I found most jarring.

    The legroom was decent, too. The retro seatback screens, on the other hand, were pretty much redundant.

    It has been revealed that it was stepping on board the 16-year-old Boeing 737-700 back to Buenos Aires that Aerolíneas Argentinas’ low-costness was most glaring. Looking at this, I would never guess this plane belonged to a flag carrier. The seats were very uncomfortable, and I think I remember they didn’t recline either.

    As for service, I don’t recall it being particularly good or particularly bad. Forgettable is probably the most accurate word.

    Industry observers note that imagine the likes of Spirit (RIP) or Ryanair calling itself a national flag carrier; that’s basically what Aerolíneas Argentinas is. I’m planning a trip with my dad and brother for February next year that includes Argentina, and I will actively avoid flying Aerolíneas, even if it means forgoing the chance to earn any Flying Blue miles and XPs.

    According to recent reports, it’s almost as if the airline has been abandoned. After all, the only real competition is low-cost airlines at LATAM — the full-service carrier which dominates South America. Who knows, maybe things will change come 2028 when it takes delivery of new Airbus A330-900s and Boeing 737 MAXs.

    If I were a power that be at SkyTeam, I’d definitely remove the airline from the alliance. And if I had my way, Aerolíneas Argentinas would be bought by LATAM, and the cherry on top would be LATAM joining SkyTeam. I should probably put a business case together for that….
