    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday.
    • Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.
    • Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., delivers his opening statement during the hearing on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

    Online safety advocates are looking to the annual defense policy bill for action on legislation to expand accountability for online platforms in cases of child sexual exploitation, as they also introduced legislation to make sure those cases aren’t forced into private arbitration.

    Senators and advocates expressed support Tuesday for legislation that would expand the ability of victims of online sexual exploitation to sue social media platforms at a hearing focused on dangers children face on the gaming platform Roblox.

    Sources indicate that the Senate Judiciary Committee’s panel on Crime and Counterterrorism held the hearing after its Chairman Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and ranking member Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., introduced a bill Monday that would ban pre-dispute arbitration agreements from affecting cases where a minor was harmed online, including by sexual exploitation.

    Hawley and Durbin also worked together on a separate bill to expand eligibility for victims of abuse to bring civil suits against online platforms that intentionally, knowingly or recklessly promoted or facilitated the abuse. It would also include penalties for certain platforms that fail to report child pornography violations on their sites.

    That bill is included in a manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill. Durbin encouraged Congress to pass the NDAA “in the closing days” of the session because “protecting children is an important part of it.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “I have a few weeks left in my service in the United States Senate,” stated Durbin, who is retiring at the end of his term in January. “I’m thinking each day it’s coming to an end, but I want it to come [to an] end the right way.”.

    The subcommittee has spent much of the 119th Congress focused on harms to children online, including from artificial intelligence chatbots.

    Tuesday’s hearing included testimony from survivors and experts on child exploitation on Roblox.

    Hawley mentioned that victims are bound by pre-dispute agreements with Roblox to settle claims through private arbitration, rather than in court.

    “They slam the courthouse door shut in their faces,” Hawley mentioned. “We’re talking about children now, child victims of sexual exploitation online are denied their day in court by the very organization that has exposed them to the content to begin with.”.

    A spokesperson for Roblox said in a statement that “safety has been central” to the platform since its launch.

    “We require age checks for chat, place consumers under 16 in age-based accounts with protective defaults, and block images and video in chat,” the spokesperson stated. “A legal position about arbitration is not a measure of a manufacturer’s safety record, and a hearing built around it fails to advance safety.”.

    Myriam Gilles, a professor of law at Northwestern University, told the panel that a 2022 law that ended forced arbitration agreements for victims of sexual assault has gaps. She remarked Roblox has argued it does not apply to online actions, just “completed physical assault” and does not apply to platforms.

    She also said that Hawley’s upcoming arbitration bill would enhance the effects of his measure regarding civil suits by making sure those suits can be heard publicly if families so choose.

    “Congress can pass laws, but if [suits] just get shunted into private arbitration, they’re doing no good in the world,” Gilles mentioned. “A right to sue that ends in secret arbitration is a right in name only.”.

    The hearing came the same day that advocates, including reality TV personality and activist Paris Hilton, held a press conference to urge House action on a bill (S 1837) that would allow individuals to bring civil suits over nonconsensual intimate depictions generated by artificial intelligence or for possession or production of deepfake porn if there was also intent to disclose the images.

    That bill passed the Senate in January but has not been taken up in the House.

Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

    That’s a solid bonus for a card at this price point, and the six month window gives you plenty of time to hit the spending requirement. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

    It has been revealed that amex cards tend to be fairly easy to get approved for if you have excellent credit. A few rules to know:.

    As you can see, this card is marketed as offering a bonus “as high as” a certain amount. The way this works, you can apply for the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card, and then find out your offer amount. Then you can decide whether you want to accept the offer or not. That’s an unconventional approach for a welcome offer. At least Amex has the “apply with confidence” feature, so there won’t be a hard pull unless you accept the offer.

    The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has a $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95. (Rates & Fees). That puts it in line with other mid-range cards.     If you decide the card isn’t working for you after the first year, you can always downgrade to the no annual fee Blue Cash Everyday Card.

    Industry observers note that I wouldn’t recommend using the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card outside the U.S. or for purchases in foreign currencies. The 2.7% foreign transaction fee will eat into your rewards (Rates & Fees). There are plenty of other cards with no foreign transaction fees that are better suited for international spending.

    The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has some excellent bonus categories, especially if you spend a lot at U.S. supermarkets and on streaming. Below is a full breakdown.

    This is the headline feature of the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, and it’s the single best cash back rate for U.S. supermarket spending that I’m aware of. You earn 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets on up to $6,000 per year in purchases (then 1%). This is the only bonus category with an earning cap.

    Recent findings suggest that to put that in perspective, if you spend $500 a month on U.S. supermarket spending, you’d earn $360 per year in cash back from this category alone. That more than covers the $95 annual fee.

    It has been revealed that note that supermarkets don’t include superstores, warehouse clubs (like Costco or Sam’s Club), or discount stores. If most of your grocery shopping happens at a traditional supermarket, this card is incredibly rewarding.

    The Amex Blue Cash Preferred also offers 6% cash back on select U.S. streaming subscriptions. The list of qualifying services is quite long and includes most of the major platforms: Netflix, Hulu, Disney+, ESPN+, HBO Max, Spotify, Apple TV, Apple Music, Amazon Music Unlimited, YouTube Premium, YouTube TV, Peacock, Sling TV, and many more.

    If you’re spending $50 to $100 a month across streaming services (which many households are these days), that 6% adds up nicely.

    The Amex Blue Cash Preferred offers 3% cash back on transit purchases, including taxis, ridesharing, parking, tolls, trains, and buses. If you commute by public transit or use rideshare services regularly, this is a solid bonus category.

    With the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, you also earn 3% cash back at eligible U.S. gas stations, with no caps. Note that this doesn’t include gas purchased at superstores, supermarkets, or warehouse clubs that sell fuel.

    For purchases that don’t fall into the bonus categories, you earn 1% cash back. This is the one weak spot of the card. At just 1% on non-bonused spending, you’ll want to pair this card with something that earns a better return on everyday purchases (more on that below).

    Recent findings suggest that with the Amex Blue Cash Preferred, you earn Reward Dollars that can be redeemed as statement credits, and there’s no minimum cash back balance required before you can redeem. It’s simple and straightforward, though it’s worth knowing that you can’t use cash back to pay your minimum payment due.

    Sources indicate that as is the case for any credit card, it’s also notable to consider the benefits and credits offered, if any. The Amex Blue Cash Preferred has a reasonable annual fee, so what are the benefits like? Well, they’re potentially pretty solid, and can help justify the annual fee….

    According to recent reports, the Amex Blue Cash Preferred offers up to $10 back per month ($120 per year) as a statement credit when you use your enrolled card to purchase a subscription, including a bundle subscription, on DisneyPlus.com, Hulu.com, or Stream.ESPN.com U.S. websites, with no minimum purchase requirement. Subscription is subject to auto-renewal. (Enrollment required).

    Another Amex Blue Cash Preferred benefit is access to Amex Presale Tickets® and Amex Reserved Tickets®, which can come in handy if you’re trying to score tickets to an in-demand concert or sporting event.

    The Amex Blue Cash Preferred also includes an introductory 0% APR offer that can give you some breathing room on purchases and balance transfers.

Just make sure you pay off your balance in full before the intro period ends, or you’ll be on the hook for interest after all.

    One benefit that doesn’t get enough attention is the Amex Offers program. This gives you access to targeted deals with a variety of retailers, just by registering your card and making an eligible purchase.

    In a recent development, different Amex cards get different offers, so having multiple Amex cards in your wallet means more chances to save. Across my Amex cards, this program saves me hundreds of dollars per year.

    Recent findings suggest that the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card has fewer travel protections than more premium Amex cards, but it does come with coverage to protect your rental car when you charge the rental to this card. The coverage applies for eligible damage or theft, and it’s secondary, so it kicks in after your own car insurance. There are some exclusions, and it doesn’t include liability coverage, so check your card benefits guide for the full details.

    Industry observers note that I tend to lean toward points-earning cards for my own spending, but I totally get why a lot of people prefer cash back. It’s simple, flexible, and you can spend it however you want, including on travel. For that crowd, the Blue Cash Preferred is one of the best options out there.

    If you’re someone who is looking to earn cash back and spends a lot at supermarkets, then the Amex Blue Cash Preferred Card is an exceptional choice, in my opinion — 6% cash back will add up quickly.

    The 6% cash back on streaming, and 3% cash back on transit and gas stations, will add up quickly as well, and up to $120 Disney streaming credit could be worth more than the annual fee.

    It has been revealed that however, this isn’t the card I would be using for your everyday spending, as you’d only earn 1% cash back in the categories that aren’t eligible for bonuses. So I’d acquire this card specifically with the intent of using it in the categories offering bonuses.

    So, let’s take a look at what other cards you should potentially be considering.

    Industry observers note that if you like the idea of an Amex cash back card but aren’t sure about paying an annual fee, the Blue Cash Everyday Card from American Express (learn more) is the no annual fee alternative where you can earn as high as $200 cash back after spending $2,000 in purchases on your latest Card in the first six months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

    Here’s how the two Blue Cash cards compare:.

    Sources indicate that in my opinion, the Blue Cash Preferred is well worth the annual fee if you spend a meaningful amount at supermarkets. The jump from 3% to 6% on U.S. supermarkets adds up fast. If you spend $500 a month at supermarkets, that extra 3% earns you $180 more per year, which nearly doubles the annual fee.

    Sources indicate that the Blue Cash Everyday does have one unique advantage: 3% cash back on U.S. online retail purchases, which the Preferred doesn’t offer. If you do a lot of online shopping and less grocery shopping, the Everyday could actually come out ahead.

    The good news is that you can always start with the Blue Cash Preferred and downgrade to the Blue Cash Everyday after the first year if the math doesn’t work out.

    In a recent development, if you’re just looking for the simplest cash back credit card, it’s tough to go wrong with the Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more). The card offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase, for a total of 2% back on every purchase. That’s a solid return on everyday spending, and you don’t have to keep track of any bonus spending categories.

    If you’re deciding between the Blue Cash Preferred and a mid-range card from another issuer, the $95 annual fee Citi Strata Premier Card (learn more) is worth considering. These two cards serve pretty different purposes, but they’re at the same price point:.

    The Blue Cash Preferred wins on supermarkets and streaming, hands down. If those are your biggest spending categories, the Blue Cash Preferred is the better card.

    It has been revealed that the Strata Premier is the more well-rounded card overall. It earns 3x points across five major categories (dining, gas, supermarkets, airfare, hotels), has no foreign transaction fees, and its ThankYou points can be transferred to airline and hotel partners for potentially much more than face value. If you travel or eat out a lot, the Strata Premier likely comes out ahead.

    One final card worth considering alongside the Blue Cash Preferred Card is the American Express® Gold Card (learn more). It has a significantly higher annual fee, but it’s unbeatable for earning rewards at U.S. supermarkets — you’ll earn transferable Membership Rewards points too, rather than cash back.

    Here’s a look at how they compare:.

    Industry observers note that the Blue Cash Preferred is the best cash back card for supermarket spending, and it’s not particularly close. If groceries and streaming are a substantial part of your monthly budget, this card can deliver serious returns, especially with the 6% rate on both categories plus the Disney streaming credit.

    The annual fee pays for itself quickly if you’re spending even a moderate amount at supermarkets. Pair it with a card like the Citi Double Cash for your non-bonused spending, and you’ve got a strong cash back setup.

    In a recent development, just keep in mind that the 1% rate on everyday purchases means this card works best as a specialist, not your only card. Use it where it shines, and let a flat-rate card handle the rest.

    #88410. The True Cost Airbus Charges For An A330neo Compared With Boeing's 787-9 Dreamliner

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1468 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    The True Cost Airbus Charges For An A330neo Compared With Boeing's 787-9 Dreamliner

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1468 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Airbus A330-900 (A330neo) and the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner are very close competitors.
    • As Simple Flying has previously highlighted, headline list figures are an unreliable method to determine the true costs and value of aircraft and aero engines.
    • According to recent reports, to understand why list prices are not particularly useful, it is necessary to understand what they are.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Airbus A330-900 (A330neo) and the Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner are very close competitors. On the face of it, the 787-9 has a much larger order book (1,493 vs 511), has a noticeably higher market value, and is a cleansheet aircraft. This could be interpreted as suggesting the 787-9 has a cost advantage over the A330-900. However, the truth is more complicated, and it allows the A330-900 to remain competitive.

    As Simple Flying has previously highlighted, headline list figures are an unreliable method to determine the true costs and value of aircraft and aero engines. To faithfully answer the headline of this article, list prices need to be set aside in favor of market prices and lease rates. The aviation industry runs on very thin margins. Consequently, averaging the costs of these two aircraft without considering the contingent variables of the airline in question will likely provide highly misleading numbers.

    According to recent reports, to understand why list prices are not particularly useful, it is necessary to understand what they are. An aircraft manufacturer’s list price is the published, baseline 'sticker price' for a new aircraft before negotiated discounts, rebates, or custom configuration changes. These are typically inflated prices where the manufacturer is essentially saying, "this is what we value our product at," even though it realistically never sells them at that price and airlines and lessors would never pay it.

    In a recent development, for an analogy, think of an airline offering the chance to win a holiday package "valued at $10,000." That figure may include estimates for tours, accommodation, flights, transfers, etc., all priced at the highest retail price. In practice, the airline would likely be utilizing spare capacity, receiving bulk discounts, and having special pricing arrangements, so it's only paying a fraction of the headline figure.

    Likewise, holidaymakers may be able to book their own analogous trip at a fraction of the cost. List prices are similar, although they may provide a starting point in complex aircraft negotiations. As discussed below, sometimes the airplane manufacturer (Airbus, Boeing) has significant bargaining power in negotiations, while at other times the balance can swing to the customer (e.g., Emirates vis-à-vis the 777-9).

    According to recent reports, currently, the market values for Boeing 787-9s and A330neos are unusually high due to production bottlenecks at Airbus and Boeing. IBA writes, "This has pushed the expected delivery dates for many recent orders as far back as early 2030. With hampered production rates, it comes as no surprise that this has, in turn, allowed for Market Values and MLRs to rally over the years." The value of widebody aircraft has grown especially fast over the last year.

    In a November 2026 patch, IBA reported, "Constrained supply is supporting trading values, with 2026 market values up 7% for the 787-9, 5% for the A350-900, 24% for the 777-300ER and 20% for the A330-300, alongside rising lease rates." This demonstrates a significant increase in market value for the older A330-300 cousin to the A330neo, but fails to include the A330neo price increase.

    Cost comparison (per IBA, My Air Trade, Green Airlines).

    Market value (oldest airframes).

    Recent findings suggest that while it's unclear how much the A330-900's market value has increased recently, its market lease rates are up by as much as 13%. The monthly market lease rate for a newly introduced Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner is around $1.05-$1.16 million, and around $900,000-$990,000 for the A330neo. At mid-age, the 787-9's rate is around $695,000-$792,000, while the A330neo is around $600,000-$756,000 per month.

    According to recent reports, in Q1 2026, for a newly delivered Airbus A330-900, IBA ascribed a market value of $118.5 million. Meanwhile, a new Boeing 787-9 is expected to trade in the region of $160 million. Overall, the new-delivery market value of a Boeing 787-9 is estimated to be in the $151–$160 million range by different industry analysts. The new-delivery market value range of an A330-900 (A330neo) is around $118.5–$119 million.

    For comparison, the market value for larger 787-10 latest-builds is around $168 million, or about $8 million more than the standard 787-9. The new value of the short 787-8 is around $116 million, or almost the same as a new A330-900. My Air Trade highlights that the oldest 787-9 is estimated at around $70.6 million, while the oldest A330-900 is valued at around $73 million.

    The oldest second-hand examples are estimated to be $47 million for the 787-8 and $95 million for the 787-10. No market values are given for the unpopular A330-800 variant, perhaps due to the limited deliveries and lack of market trading for the aircraft. Separately, the market values for the A380 are very low. The oldest A380s are estimated to be worth $12 million, and the most valuable are around $45 million. Put another way, a new A330-900 is worth around 3x-10x that of the world's remaining A380s.

    Recent findings suggest that the A330-900 and Boeing 787-9 compete on the market for a similar (but not the same) market segment. These aircraft are similar in length and have comparable typical 3-class seating capacities: 260-300 for the A330-900 and 250-290 for the 787-9. The maximum seating is around 460 and 420, respectively. In practice, the 787-9s are typically assigned more to flagship routes than the A330neo and are configured with an average of 264 seats, compared with the A330-900's denser 281-seat average.

    They have almost identical maximum take-off weights (251 tonnes vs 254 tonnes) and are both very competitive in terms of cargo capacity. The Boeing 787-9 is deemed to have a modest advantage in range, although that only matters in edge cases, as most missions are well within the A330neo's maximum range. When it comes to fuel burn, it depends heavily on payload, configuration, and range. As a rule, the 787-9's fuel advantage grows with longer ranges.

    One of the biggest differences is that the 787-9 is a fundamentally cleansheet composite aircraft, while the A330neo is a comprehensive update on the 1980s-designed A330. The A330neo has fresh engines, new wings, new avionics, and other updates, but it still has an older architecture and a mostly aluminum fuselage.

    It is impossible to put a precise figure on how much the A330-900 and 787-9 cost to operate relative to each other. Too much is contingent. Even setting aside that these aircraft are better optimized for different routes and missions, many airline-specific factors matter. One important factor is the composition of the airline's overall fleet.

    Recent findings suggest that if an airline (e.g., Delta) also operates older A330s and new A350s, it can significantly increase fleet commonality and significantly reduce maintenance and training expenses. Airbus claims up to 95% commonality in A330ceo/A330neo spare parts, including substantial tooling commonality and the same pilot type rating between the generations. Airbus also claims, "Today, the A321neo and the A330neo have proven to deliver up to 30% lower operating costs when operated together.".

    By contrast, the benefits of commonality are more limited with airlines operating the Boeing 777 and Boeing 787, with no common type rating and the 787 requiring dedicated tooling. Commonality with the predecessor Boeing 767 is even more limited. However, there is a very high benefit to operating parallel fleets of 787-8s and 787-10s. The value of commonality can drive major airlines (e.g., Southwest, Ryanair) to only operate one family of aircraft.

    Industry observers note that as shown by the market prices, the A330-900 is around $30–40 million cheaper in new aircraft value and has a lower lease rate per month. This suggests the A330-900 benefits from lower capital, financing, and leasing costs. But this hides a major distortion. This is the secondary-market value, not the cost at which they were purchased. The largest order (cumulative) for the A330-900 is by Cathay Pacific for 41, while the largest cumulative order for the 787-9 is 132 by United (and 221 for all Boeing 787 variants).

    As a general rule, an airline purchasing aircraft in the single digits may be in a negotiating position to get around 25% off the list price (with massive variation). An airline ordering 50–100 aircraft could be able to negotiate a 45–55% discount off the list price. These purchase price differences disappear once they hit the secondary market.

    In a recent development, in practice, airlines can bundle orders, as when Qatar Airways ordered 130 Dreamliners and 30 Boeing 777-9s with options for 50 Boeing 787/777X airliners. All this is to say that the cost of operating an A330-900 may be higher or lower than that of the 787-9, depending on the circumstances. Using some back-of-the-envelope math, both airliners will likely cost around $13,000 per flight hour to operate, plus or minus a few thousand dollars. The winner will be highly contingent.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Airlines and Israir Airlines have just announced intends to partner for flights between the United States and Israel.
    • American and Israir are launching a commercial partnership focused on enhanced travel options between Israel and the United States.
    • For context, as of March 27, 2027, American plans to resume flights between New York and Tel Aviv, using the Boeing 777-200ER.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Airlines and Israir Airlines have just announced intends to partner for flights between the United States and Israel. For now don’t expect huge implications, but over time, this has the potential to evolve.

    American and Israir are launching a commercial partnership focused on enhanced travel options between Israel and the United States. The partnership is expected to expand in phases, delivering some benefits to customers. American plans to resume flights to Tel Aviv (TLV) as of late March 2027.

    How is this partnership expected to play out?

    For context, as of March 27, 2027, American plans to resume flights between New York and Tel Aviv, using the Boeing 777-200ER. Israir operates five weekly flights between Tel Aviv and New York, using an Airbus A330-200 (funny enough, the airline flies ex-American A330s, which the airline retired shortly after the start of the pandemic).

    For those curious about the interiors of Israir’s A330s, below is a video of them (sorry, I don’t know what’s going on in the video, but I haven’t otherwise been able to find a cabin video).

    Here’s how American’s SVP of Alliances, Anmol Bhargava, describes this:.

    In a recent development, “American looks forward to building a relationship with Israir that will give customers the convenient, well-connected travel options they desire. As we prepare to resume service between New York and Tel Aviv next spring, this partnership will help us deliver a stronger customer proposition in the market and create more opportunities for Israir’s travelers to connect beyond our JFK gateway.”.

    The dynamics of this partnership are interesting. There are a few things to keep in mind:.

    When it comes to the latest partnership between American and Israir, here’s what’s I find noteworthy:.

    All-in-all, this is a pretty casual partnership. There’s no real downside here for American, since the carrier might just pick up a little bit of revenue on connecting Israir passengers beyond New York. Meanwhile Israir has a better framework for selling tickets beyond New York, which helps the carrier expand its potential customer base. But it is interesting how the codeshare is one-sided for now….

    American Airlines and Israir Airlines are launching a partnership for flights between the United States and Israel. Israir will be codesharing on American’s flight between New York and Tel Aviv (when that resumes in late March 2027, in theory), while American will have an interline agreement with Israir, allowing Israir passengers to connect on American flights beyond New York.

    Sources indicate that we may see a closer level of cooperation between the two airlines in the future, including possible AAdvantage perks, but nothing has been finalized there yet. I wouldn’t read too much into this partnership for now, and think it falls more in the category of “better than nothing,” rather than anything beyond that.

    Tech Report: Amex Blue Cash Everyday Review: A No Annual Fee Card With Solid Bonus Categories

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2417 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • American Express is best known for its points-earning cards, but the Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express proves that Amex can do cash back well too.
    • Sources indicate that if you’re looking for a simple card that earns a solid return at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers, this one is worth a look.
    • This post is my in-depth Blue Cash Everyday Card review, so I’ll cover the bonus categories, the credits and perks, and how this card compares to both the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express and the Citi Double Cash® Card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    American Express is best known for its points-earning cards, but the Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express proves that Amex can do cash back well too.

    Sources indicate that if you’re looking for a simple card that earns a solid return at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers, this one is worth a look. It has no annual fee (Rates & Fees), a decent welcome bonus, a great intro APR offer, and some useful bonus categories that cover a good chunk of everyday spending.

    This post is my in-depth Blue Cash Everyday Card review, so I’ll cover the bonus categories, the credits and perks, and how this card compares to both the Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express and the Citi Double Cash® Card.

    Review: Learn more about the Blue Cash Everyday® Card from American Express.

    First, here’s an overview of the Amex Blue Cash Everyday benefits and value proposition, from fees, to rewards, to the welcome bonus:.

    I also put together my list of pros and cons for the Blue Cash Everyday Card:.

    When applying for a credit card, obviously the welcome offer, eligibility rules, and fees, are major considerations. So below I’ll cover the details of that for the Amex Blue Cash Everyday.

    It has been revealed that the Amex Blue Cash Everyday is offering the following welcome bonus: You may be eligible for as high as $200 cash back after spending $2,000 in purchases on your new Card in the first 6 months. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer. Cash back is received as Reward Dollars, redeemable for statement credit or for other select options. Terms Apply.

    That’s a reasonable bonus for a no annual fee card, and the spending requirement is low enough that most people should be able to hit it. However, it’s also not that much to get excited about, compared to some of the other welcome offers out there.

    Recent findings suggest that amex cards tend to be fairly easy to get approved for if you have excellent credit. Here are the main rules to be aware of:.

    Amex also has a pre-application eligibility tool that lets you check whether you’ll be approved for the card without any impact on your credit score. This is worth using if you’re not sure that you’ll qualify.

    It has been revealed that the Blue Cash Everyday Card has no annual fee. Not the first year, not ever. That alone makes it worth considering as a long-term card in your wallet, even if it’s not your primary spender.

    Holding no annual fee cards long term is also a great way to help your credit score. About 30% of your score comes from credit utilization (the more available credit you have but don’t use, the better), and 15% comes from credit history length (the older your average account age, the better). A no annual fee card you keep open for years helps on both fronts.

    According to recent reports, the Blue Cash Everyday Card does have foreign transaction fees (2.7%) (Rates & Fees), so I wouldn’t use it for purchases in foreign currencies. Stick to domestic spending with this one, and find a card with no foreign transaction fees if you’ll be spending time abroad.

    The Amex Blue Cash Everyday has three main bonus categories, each earning 3% cash back on up to $6,000 per year in purchases (then 1%).

    With the Blue Cash Everyday, you earn 3% back at U.S. supermarkets on up to $6,000 per year (then 1%). Earning 3% back at supermarkets with no annual fee is a solid deal, and this is one of the better no annual fee cards for U.S. supermarket spending.

    Sources indicate that as with most grocery bonus categories, this generally won’t include warehouse clubs (like Costco), superstores (like Walmart or Target), convenience stores, or discount stores. Traditional supermarkets and grocery chains are what you’re looking for.

    With the Blue Cash Everyday, you also earn 3% back at U.S. gas stations on up to $6,000 per year (then 1%). This is one of the better no annual fee cards for gas station spending.

    This is the bonus category that makes the Blue Cash Everyday stand out from its siblings. You earn 3% back on U.S. online retail purchases on up to $6,000 per year (then 1%). This covers purchases made on a website or app from a U.S. retail merchant that sells physical goods directly to consumers.

    Sources indicate that given how much shopping happens online these days, this can be a really valuable category. You won’t find this bonus on many other cards.

    For purchases outside the bonus categories, you earn 1% cash back. This is where the card falls short. At just 1% on non-bonused spending, you’ll definitely want to pair this with a card that offers a better return on everyday purchases.

    With the Amex Blue Cash Everyday, you earn Reward Dollars that can be redeemed as statement credits at a rate of 1.0 cents per point, and there’s no minimum cash back balance required before you can redeem.

    It’s simple and straightforward, though it’s worth knowing that you can’t use cash back to pay your minimum payment due.

    Industry observers note that benefits and credits can certainly help with justifying holding onto credit cards. In the case of the Amex Blue Cash Everyday, you wouldn’t expect very valuable perks, given the card’s lack of an annual fee. However, it’s an area where I’d say the card actually exceeds expectations, and offers solid value.

    According to recent reports, the Blue Cash Everyday offers up to $7 back per month (up to $84 per year) as a statement credit when you use your enrolled Blue Cash Everyday to purchase a subscription, including a bundle subscription, on DisneyPlus.com, Hulu.com, or Stream.ESPN.com U.S. websites, with no minimum purchase requirement. Subscriptions are subject to auto-renewal. If you already pay for any of those services, this is an easy credit to use. (Enrollment required).

    You can also earn up to $15 per month (up to $180 per year) in statement credits when you purchase Home Chef meal solutions online with your Blue Cash Everyday Card. If you use Home Chef, this is a significant benefit. If you don’t, it’s probably not worth signing up just for the credit. (Enrollment required).

    The Blue Cash Everyday Card also offers 0% intro APR on purchases and balance transfers for 15 months from the date of account opening. After that, the variable APR is presently between 19.74% - 28.74% (Rates & Fees).

    I generally recommend avoiding financing purchases through credit cards. But if a short-term 0% APR opportunity can help you manage a large purchase and you can pay it off before the rate increases, it’s a nice option to have.

    Another card benefit is access to Amex Presale Tickets® and Amex Reserved Tickets®, which can come in handy if you’re trying to score tickets to an in-demand concert or sporting event.

    Recent findings suggest that every Amex card gives you access to the Amex Offers program, which provides targeted deals with a variety of retailers. Different cards get different offers, so having multiple Amex cards means more chances to save.

    According to recent reports, I try to have as many Amex cards as possible specifically to take advantage of this. Having a no annual fee card like this is ideal, since the card isn’t costing you anything, but you’re still getting access to potentially valuable offers.

    Recent findings suggest that the Amex Blue Cash Everyday comes with coverage to protect your rental car when you charge the rental to this card. The coverage applies for eligible damage or theft, and it’s secondary, so it kicks in after your own car insurance. There are some exclusions, and it doesn’t include liability coverage, so check your card benefits guide for the full details.

    Car rental loss and damage insurance: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Manufacturer. Car Rental Loss or Damage Coverage is offered through American Express Travel Related Services Company, Inc.

    The Blue Cash Everyday Card also offers purchase protection of up to $1,000 per covered purchase for up to 90 days from the purchase date. You need to pay with the card in order to take advantage of this coverage.

    The Amex Blue Cash Everyday Card is a solid no annual fee cash back card with useful bonus categories at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers. The 3% rate in those categories is strong for a no annual fee card, and the Disney streaming credits, Home Chef credits, and Amex Offers add extra value on top.

    While there are several reasons to consider the Blue Cash Everyday Card, there are also a couple of alternatives that I think are better for most people.

    If you generally like the idea of the Blue Cash Everyday Card, there might still be a better play here. The Blue Cash Preferred® Card from American Express (learn more) is the premium version of the card, and it could be worth applying for it instead (Enrollment is required for select benefits).

    Recent findings suggest that the big question is whether the Preferred’s $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95. annual fee (Rates & Fees) is worth the upgrade. If you spend at least $267 per month at U.S. supermarkets, the extra 3% (the Preferred earns 6% cash back at U.S. supermarkets on up to $6,000 per year in purchases, then 1%) on groceries alone will cover the fee. The Preferred also adds 6% cash back on select U.S. streaming and 3% on transit, which the Everyday doesn’t offer.

    Recent findings suggest that on the flip side, the Everyday has two things the Preferred doesn’t: 3% on U.S. online retail purchases and a 0% intro APR offer. If you do a lot of online shopping and not as much grocery shopping, the Everyday could be the better card.

    It has been revealed that one nice thing is that you could start with the Blue Cash Preferred (with a $0 intro annual fee for the first year, then $95.), and if the math doesn’t work out, downgrade to the Blue Cash Everyday after year one. That way you get the bigger welcome bonus and can test the higher earning rates.

    While there are lots to like about the Blue Cash Everyday, it’s also not particularly well-rounded if you’re looking for an all-in-one cash back credit card.

    Sources indicate that the card offers 3% cash back at U.S. supermarkets, U.S. gas stations, and U.S. online retail purchases (up to certain limits), but on other purchases you’ll earn 1% cash back.

    Industry observers note that everyone will have to crunch the numbers for themselves, but 1% cash back is pretty uncompetitive nowadays for savvy consumers. For example, the no annual fee Citi Double Cash® Card (learn more) offers 1% cash back when you make a purchase, and 1% cash back when you pay for that purchase (in the form of ThankYou points).

    Sources indicate that the Blue Cash Everyday wins in its bonus categories, earning 3% at supermarkets, gas stations, and online retailers compared to the Double Cash’s flat 2%. But the Double Cash wins everywhere else, earning 2% on all purchases versus just 1%.

    Recent findings suggest that if your spending is heavily concentrated in supermarkets, gas, and online shopping, the Blue Cash Everyday will earn you more. If your spending is more spread out across lots of different categories, the Double Cash’s flat 2% on everything will likely come out ahead.

    It has been revealed that the Double Cash also has a major advantage in flexibility. Its ThankYou points can be transferred to airline and hotel partners (in conjunction with a premium Citi card like the Citi Strata Premier® Card), giving those points the potential to be worth well more than 2 cents each. The Blue Cash Everyday’s rewards are purely cash back.

    The ideal setup? Have both. Use the Blue Cash Everyday for supermarkets, gas, and online retail where it earns 3%, and the Double Cash for everything else at 2%.

    Industry observers note that I think the Blue Cash Everyday is a very decent cash back card with bonus categories most spenders can take advantage of. The card’s main weakness is the 1% rate on everything outside the bonus categories — and even on those categories once you reach the annual cap. For that reason, I’d recommend pairing it with a flat-rate card like the Citi Double Cash (2% on everything) to fill in the gaps. Together, they make a simple, effective, no annual fee credit card cash back setup.

    If you find yourself spending more at supermarkets over time, you can always upgrade to the Blue Cash Preferred for that 6% supermarket rate. But for a no annual fee, low-maintenance starting point, the Blue Cash Everyday is a great choice.

    #88407. Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1001 w)

    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Hill GOP looking to trim White House's $50 billion aviation ask

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1001 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday.
    • Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s upcoming ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.
    • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy conducts a news conference on the recent nationwide ground stop after meeting with Senate Republicans in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Senate Republicans poured cold water Tuesday on the administration’s upcoming ask for a $50.1 billion emergency air traffic control and airport infrastructure package, arguing much of it has little to do with the immediate problems that led to a nationwide ground stop on Friday.

    Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought last week asked for $30.1 billion before Duffy voiced support for the rest of the funds at a Friday night press conference on the ground stop.

    The original ask contained roughly $12 billion that was tied directly to air traffic control upgrades, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., noted, with the remainder going toward long-sought airport terminal and other upgrades to aging aviation facilities.

    Duffy and Vought laid out in a letter to House and Senate appropriators on Tuesday what the extra $20 billion would be for — half for construction of five new air route traffic control centers, and half for construction, replacement and improvement of up to 140 air traffic control towers.

    They justified the increased demand because of the “urgent need” that became evident after the ground stop. Duffy and Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford fanned out across the Capitol to try to sell the request, including a stop at Senate Republicans’ weekly policy lunch.

    But it swiftly became evident that their own allies on Capitol Hill want more and better justification for why so much extra money is needed.

    Not only are there concerns that much of the request would go to terminal reconstruction and other longer-term projects, but lawmakers keep noting the FAA hasn’t yet spent about $8 billion out of the initial $12.5 billion “down payment” on air traffic control modernization provided in last year’s budget reconciliation law.

    “I don’t think the full $50 billion will be funded,” Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, stated Tuesday. “What we just discussed there, and what I expressed, is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.”.

    Still, Cruz stated the administration had done a “good job” with the initial $12.5 billion modernization initiative so far and he expected to see continued bipartisan support for the effort.

    Senate Republicans are considering adding additional aviation funds through a filibuster-proof reconciliation bill, a process that could begin as soon as this week with a floor “vote-a-rama” on a resolution to unlock that process. Cruz stated that while reconciliation could be the vehicle used, additional aviation funds need to be “safety-focused.”.

    Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said after the lunch with Duffy and Bedford that he expects Congress will look at a package more in the $10 billion to $30 billion range.

    Recent findings suggest that for his part, Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said the airline industry itself should foot at least a portion of the bill, considering how much federal support the carriers have received over the years.

    Sources indicate that “I don't understand why the airline industry doesn't pay for it. We give them unbelievable amounts of money,” Scott said, adding that he doesn’t like adding to the deficit and is “not significant on government running things.”.

    Duffy explained the need for the high price tag as the result of decades of pent-up demand that are now threatening major disruptions and safety risks to the traveling public.

    Sources indicate that “This has never been done. To be clear, we are keeping planes safe in the sky, and we are switching out equipment that’s been a problem for decades,” he mentioned. “I and the president have decided we are going to lean in and fix it.”.

    He called the effort a “historic investment” reflecting the ways air travel has changed since much of the nation’s infrastructure was built — noting that the newest tower was constructed in 1969 and much of the software being used is from the 1990s. Still, Duffy stated, on the current course of funding, it would take 300 years to replace every U.S. tower.

    According to recent reports, “I'm not going to tell [Congress] how to do their work, but I'm telling everybody what we need,” Duffy mentioned. “And whether it's a party-line vote or if it's a bipartisan vote, I do think this is one moment in a very charged political environment — one moment where almost all Americans and bipartisan members of both bodies are kind of in agreement that we should lean in to do this.”.

    Even as Duffy petitioned for additional funds Tuesday, he noted that the “root cause” of the equipment instability that made the ground stop necessary is still unclear as investigators analyze the router that caused the problem.

    A “routine switchover” from old copper wires to digital fiber in the telecommunications system “started to create complications in our network,” Duffy explained Tuesday.

    The telecommunications transition includes the conversion of thousands of routers to what are known as Juniper devices — a process being undertaken by contractor L3Harris Technologies. Duffy and Bedford explained that 68 other routers had been converted without incident prior to the problematic switchover Friday.

    Bedford said Tuesday that use of the router that officials have identified as the source of the system instability has been suspended “and we've disabled the ones that are out there.”.

    According to recent reports, the decision to suspend use of the router followed an inquiry sent to the agency by Senate Commerce Committee Democrats a day prior. “With thousands of conversions remaining, FAA must address outstanding safety and reliability concerns before expanding installation,” they wrote.

    Bedford said he was “highly confident” that similar problems wouldn’t erupt again. “Every element of this is going to be analyzed to see what we learn here and make sure that it doesn't get repeated,” he said.

    David Jordan, Lia Chien and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

    #88406. Why Airlines Accept The Airbus A321XLR's Heavier 101.5-Tonne Maximum Takeoff Weight On Flights Shorter Than An Hour

    📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1555 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Airlines Accept The Airbus A321XLR's Heavier 101.5-Tonne Maximum Takeoff Weight On Flights Shorter Than An Hour

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1555 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that the Airbus A321XLR has helped open a new chapter in long-and-thin aviation.
    • Despite its impressive capabilities, airlines have been known to put the XLR to work on connections that span a fraction of the distance the aircraft can actually fly.
    • On the surface, the A321XLR and standard Airbus A321neo appear almost identical.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that the Airbus A321XLR has helped open a new chapter in long-and-thin aviation. As the latest variant to appear in the Airbus A320 family, the XLR — or Extra Long Range — has taken the crown as the longest-range commercial narrowbody. Simply put, it has provided operators with arguably the best means yet of efficiently serving long-haul routes that would otherwise be unsuited to larger, widebody aircraft.

    Despite its impressive capabilities, airlines have been known to put the XLR to work on connections that span a fraction of the distance the aircraft can actually fly. In some extreme cases, these do not even stretch to an hour of flight time. But modifications were needed for the XLR to earn its title, and these added weight. So for those opting to schedule their XLRs on such short routes, the reality is accepting the penalties of operating a heavier plane than might normally do the job. Nonetheless, carriers continue to do so anyway, which raises the question: Why?

    On the surface, the A321XLR and standard Airbus A321neo appear almost identical. They share a score of common features, from their engines to their capacities to their basic dimensions, including wingspans and the same fuselage length, width, and height. A bystander could not be blamed for mistaking one for the other as a result.

    Airbus deliberately developed the duo this way too, with these retained features making it operationally viable for airlines to operate both variants in their fleets. Unchanged dimensions mean the same gate spacing and ground equipment can be used at airports, for instance. It also simplifies crew training, as pilots can fly either variant without having to train for an entirely separate type rating.

    Select A321XLR and A321neo specifications, from Airbus:.

    4,700 nautical miles (8,700 km).

    4,000 nautical miles (7,400 km).

    146 feet, 0 inches (44.51 meters).

    146 feet, 0 inches (44.51 meters).

    117 feet, 5 inches (35.80 meters).

    117 feet, 5 inches (35.80 meters).

    38 feet, 8 inches (11.76 meters).

    38 feet, 8 inches (11.76 meters).

    CFM LEAP-1A / Pratt & Whitney PW1100G.

    CFM LEAP-1A / Pratt & Whitney PW1100G.

    There are key differences between the two, which is why the XLR has a stronger range and higher maximum takeoff weight. The range is largely enabled by the addition of a permanent 3,407.82-US gallon (12,900-3liter) rear center tank on the XLR, which also explains the increased weight; Airbus has also developed an updated fuel system and outfitted the variant with necessary structural reinforcements. Ultimately, this has pushed the XLR’s maximum range to 4,700 nautical miles (8,700 km) — which is a notable step up on the NEO’s.

    Because of this, any instance where an airline chooses to use the A321XLR on a short-haul hop may seem counterintuitive. Indeed, the XLR was specifically designed to increase the A320 family's top range. Even so, many airlines do use the variant for this purpose in practice.

    In a recent development, air Canada uses its XLRs in part to connect Ottawa Macdonald-Cartier International Airport (YOW) and Toronto Pearson International Airport (YYZ), as well as Montréal-Trudeau International Airport (YUL) and Toronto, for instance. Each of these journeys lasts roughly 39 and 53 minutes, respectively, spanning between 197 nautical miles (364 km) and 274 nautical miles (507 km). Concurrently, the carrier also services its almost nine-hour Toronto to Tenerife South Airport (TFS) route using XLRs.

    Across the Atlantic, Ireland’s Aer Lingus XLRs flew more than 300 flights exceeding 3,100 miles (2,694 nautical miles or 4,989 km), alongside over 200 flights of 1,250 miles (1,086 nautical miles or 2,012 km) or fewer, in July this year, according to aviation data platform Avi-Go. These included Dublin Airport (DUB) to Nashville International Airport (BNA), scheduled at nine hours and 20 minutes, but also Dublin to London Heathrow Airport (LHR) and Dublin to Josep Tarradellas Barcelona–El Prat Airport (BCN), lasting just 48 minutes and one hour and 50 minutes, respectively. Needless to say, the XLR is by no means solely used for its range in either case.

    Industry observers note that air Canada and Aer Lingus are not alone, though. It is common practice among A321XLR operators to run the models on diverse routes with wide-ranging flight times and distances. At least, this is the case as it stands.

    Based on data from aviation analyst Cirium covering last July, American Airlines, Saudia, and Wizz Air were among the handful of XLR operators that were doing just that. The former flew its XLRs on journeys spanning the 540- to 1,079-nautical mile (1,000- to 1,999-km) and 2,700 to 3,239-nautical mile (5,000- to 5,999-km) brackets, as well as everything in between. Interestingly, these figures indicated Iberia — the XLR’s launch customer back in October 2024 — was the only carrier to exclusively use the variant for connections in the highest 2,700- to 3,239-nautical mile (5,000- to 5,999-km) and 3,240- to 3,779-nautical mile (6,000- to 6,999-km) brackets over the course of the month.

    Airbus A321XLR operators as of mid-November:.

    In other words, the carrier that has had the most time to incorporate the aircraft into its fleet appeared to be the one getting the most out of the XLR’s range most frequently. That is not surprising, though, given Airbus has only begun delivering the model in the past few years. By our count, just 61 models had been delivered to 11 carriers as of the time of writing in November, out of more than 500 orders placed.

    As such, those tasked with fitting the A321XLR into wider schedules have only recently benefited from the jets actually being on hand. Although orders placed years in advance will have given time to prepare, there is little replacement for real-world experience — especially since the XLR is, in many ways, unmatched by anything that has come before it.

    Industry observers note that in Iberia’s case, the XLR has appeared more capable than anticipated. “[It’s] even better than originally planned in terms of stage length,” chief executive Marco Antonio Trujillo remarked previously. “In fact, we are operating currently to the Caribbean, San Juan and Santo Domingo, where initially we were not thinking that the range could get over there.”.

    According to recent reports, on the flip side, Air Canada had planned to introduce XLRs between Toronto and London Heathrow this year. However, the Canadian flag carrier pulled the type before it could even debut on the service, instead opting to stick with narrowbodies for the time being. All of this goes to say, planning in advance is one thing, but meeting operational requirements in real time can be another story altogether.

    This can also explain why widebodies are sometimes used for surprisingly short journeys. Where the A321XLR’s capacity makes it an ideal, like-for-like replacement for other narrowbodies and the A321neo in particular, sometimes that is not even enough.

    Several short-haul services this year were scheduled to be flown by widebodies, as flagged by industry publication Aerospace Global News, which are traditionally associated with long-haul routes. Not least, the Airbus A350 — itself known for carrying out the longest flights on offer today — was deployed on several intra-European flights, as shown below. Similarly, the double-decker Airbus A380 saw use within Asia on a sub-six-hour connection that would technically fail to qualify as long-haul by definition.

    Select widebody-operated short-haul routes scheduled for this year, from Aerospace Global News:.

    Montreal (YUL) — Quebec City (YQB).

    Helsinki (HEL) — London Heathrow (LHR).

    1,001 nautical miles (1,853 km).

    Singapore (SIN) — Shanghai (PVG).

    2,049 nautical miles (3,794 km).

    It has been revealed that as to why such huge aircraft are selected for flights that do not quite match up to their capabilities, there are several reasons. Demand, for example, may call for more seats and make a bigger jet the more viable option. Airport slot constraints may similarly play a part, leaving airlines having to move greater numbers of passengers at once. The same factors apply to the XLR, which is designed to offer carriers a lower-risk alternative when demand isn't there to support running a widebody. No doubt, that also stretches to opening up new so-called long and thin routes, although discovering these will take time, as we are seeing today.

    At the core of all the decision-making as to which aircraft to use on which route, when and how often, and so on, is the simple fact that a plane sitting out of action on the ground is a plane not generating revenue. Whether it's a narrowbody or a widebody, using it is better than leaving it idle while waiting for the perfect deployment. Add in factors such as demand, and the reasons an aircraft type may not appear to match the route distance pile up.

    In the case of the A321XLR, Airbus has created a model as impressive for its flexibility as it is for its range. Yes, it can match several widebodies in distance, replacing them if needed due to lackluster demand. It can also fill in or complement fellow narrowbodies when required, thanks to its commonality with the A321neo.

    The caveat is the weight penalty, which is most noticeable on shorter routes. Nonetheless, airlines have clearly deemed it an acceptable trade-off to keep both their routes and jets active, and thus generating revenue in turn.

    Lufthansa Management Threatens To Massively Shrink Airline, Lay Off Employees

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, lufthansa is the “flagship” airline of Lufthansa Group, yet somehow, is the least profitable airline in the whole organization.
    • Unfortunately things haven’t turned out so great.
    • Recent findings suggest that how is that working out?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, lufthansa is the “flagship” airline of Lufthansa Group, yet somehow, is the least profitable airline in the whole organization. 2026 was supposed to be an exciting turnaround year for Lufthansa, as it’s even the carrier’s 100th anniversary.

    Unfortunately things haven’t turned out so great. Earlier this year, the carrier dealt with massive labor issues, and back-to-back-to-back strikes. Just a few months ago, the firm’s senior management claimed it wanted to turn over a newly introduced leaf with labor relations, and stop fighting with employees, so that it could find long term solutions.

    Recent findings suggest that how is that working out? Well, Lufthansa pilots are just days from possibly being able to strike again, no agreement has been reached for long term peace with employees, and management is threatening to massively shrink its mainline operation. In other words, it’s just another day at Lufthansa!

    Industry observers note that lufthansa and its pilots have been in negotiations for quite some time over the future of the organization. As you’d expect, broadly speaking, negotiations revolve around pay and future flying opportunities. As you’d expect at any airline, employees want as much flying as possible, and as massive of a fleet as possible, since that’s what maximizes their compensation.

    The issue with Lufthansa Group management is that the company’s solution to everything is to simply create fresh, low cost subsidiaries. And if Lufthansa Group management doesn’t like the terms with its subsidiaries, then it just shuts down the subsidiaries and creates new ones.

    So that brings us to the current problem. Essentially, Lufthansa’s problem is that the airline doesn’t make money on short haul flights, given high costs and intense competition. So we’ve seen the carrier increasingly outsourcing this flying to Lufthansa City Airlines, a subsidiary with lower operating costs, operating the same kinds of planes as you’ll see in the mainline fleet.

    Industry observers note that lufthansa is asking its pilots to accept wage freezes, and is promising a certain level of career development opportunities. Pilots aren’t happy with what’s being proposed, so what’s Lufthansa’s solution?

    Sources indicate that management is reportedly proposing a new initiative to the supervisory board, which would see the core Lufthansa brand massively reduce its regional flying, and largely outsource this to lower cost operations, like Lufthansa City Airlines. The idea would be to make Lufthansa primarily a long haul airline, and then have much of the short haul flying be operated by a subsidiary.

    It has been revealed that lufthansa’s mainline fleet right now consists of 260+ planes, with another 120+ planes on order. One proposal would see the mainline fleet reduced to 100 long haul aircraft and 100 short haul aircraft, with other planes being assigned to Lufthansa City Airlines.

    One radical proposal could even see Lufthansa exclusively have a long haul fleet and ditch short haul flying, though it’s noted that this isn’t the most likely scenario, and it could take several years for something like that to be implemented.

    Sources indicate that keep in mind that going back to 2017, Lufthansa had guaranteed pilots a minimum fleet size of 325 aircraft, but it terminated that agreement at the end of 2021. So it’s really hard for employees to trust any promises by management, when they can just be terminated.

    There’s no denying that labor relations can be incredibly challenging, and that the economics of intra-Europe flying are also tough, when you have competitors like Ryanair, though Lufthansa doesn’t face nearly as much competition on that front as other carriers. Then again, Frankfurt (FRA) and Munich (MUC) aren’t exactly massively leisure destinations either.

    Sources indicate that most airline employees want their company to succeed, and just want to be compensated fairly. Admittedly economics don’t always align. But what I find incredibly toxic is the approach taken by Lufthansa management. Let’s compare it to a marriage (which I think is a fair way to view the relationship between management and employees, since they’re “stuck” with one another).

    It has been revealed that lufthansa’s approach is to constantly threaten employees by saying that “if you don’t do what we want, we’ll just get rid of you.” That’s simply not a good faith way to approach things. Why would Lufthansa employees trust management, when they’ve repeatedly torn up contracts, and shown employees they simply don’t care? It would be like threatening to leave your spouse every time you have an concern, rather than trying to find a solution.

    It has been revealed that nothing against Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr personally, but I don’t understand how the board thinks he’s the best person for the job. Where’s the accountability for the endless management mistakes that have horribly impacted Lufthansa’s bottom line? Lufthansa’s employees are paying the price for the lack of success that comes as a result of all of Lufthansa’s errors, from the botched Allegris rollout, to Lufthansa’s very bad luck with new aircraft orders.

    And before anyone states “oh, but the unions,” contrast what has happened at Lufthansa Group to what has happened at Air France-KLM, under the leadership of Ben Smith. Smith has now been CEO at Air France for over eight years, and there hasn’t been a single strike under his leadership. Under the previous Air France-KLM CEO, there were endless strikes, and the situation got so bad that senior executives were being chased up a fence and having their clothes ripped off.

    Industry observers note that this reveals that good labor relations absolutely can happen, balancing the needs of employees and the organization. But it requires showing employees that you actually care about the company and their future. What was one of Smith’s first orders of business when he took the job at Air France-KLM? He eliminated Joon, the low cost carrier at the airline that was supposed to basically be a labor arbitrage opportunity. That was a way to show employees how much he respected them, and that he wanted a fair agreement, rather than one that would undermine them.

    Meanwhile Spohr’s solution to literally everything is to just threaten to start latest subsidiaries or shut down existing subsidiaries. The irony is that Spohr started his career as a pilot, so you’d think he’d have respect for employees, having been on the other side. But clearly once he became senior management, his love for aviation turned into disdain for employees.

    A few months ago, Lufthansa management claimed it wanted to turn over a new leaf when it comes to labor relations. That didn’t last long, because now the airline is back to its “do what we say or we’ll create a new subsidiary” approach.

    I don’t have a strong opinion on the exact negotiations as such. Obviously it’s a tough time for aviation, and intra-Europe flying is challenging. But if you ask me, the toxicity that has been created by Lufthansa management due to the lack of good faith negotiations just can’t be undone.

    If your only solution to everything is “oh, we’ll create a newly introduced subsidiary,” and if that doesn’t work, maybe it’s time for a new strategy. The fact that American CEO Robert Isom and Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr still have their jobs are two of the industry’s greatest mysteries.

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • It has been revealed that I visited last month and saw the very enjoyable exhibition American Prospects and Landscape Photography, 1839 to Today.
    • On “Wry and Wistful Landscapes at Kansas City’s Splendid Nelson-Atkins Museum”.

    According to recent reports, ‘E verything’s Up to Date in Kansas City” — that few minutes of pure effervescence in Oklahoma refers to Kansas City circa 1907, when it was in the middle of its version of the City Beautiful movement. Fresh boulevards, new, fancy neighborhoods, hundreds of fountains, and much more were in the works. The sparkle of a new art museum was in the civic eye, too. The Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art didn’t open its doors until 1933, but better late than never. It’s an essential visit for art lovers.

    It has been revealed that I visited last month and saw the very enjoyable exhibition American Prospects and Landscape Photography, 1839 to Today. It presents Joel Sternfeld’s lovely, often sad, wry, late-1970s and early-1980s landscape photographs in the context of the American landscape-photography genre. I love Sternfeld’s work. Born in 1944, he was the cutting-edge photographer who took color landscape photography mainstream, mostly through American Prospects, his portfolio of photographs published in book form in 1987. Color? Cutting-edge in the ’80s? Well, 1987 is about to be 40 years ago, so it qualifies as days of yore, and what has became American Prospects started in the late ’70s, when Sternfeld started an epic road trip to make art about Americans and the land. Landscape photography was, à la Ansel Adams, commonly in black and white, thought to evoke grandeur and mystery. What pushed Sternfeld to color was the advent of Kodak Vericolor III film in the 1970s. It delivered accurate, vibrant color and was good for various lighting and especially skin tones.

    Brian T. Allen is National Review’s art critic.

    On “Wry and Wistful Landscapes at Kansas City’s Splendid Nelson-Atkins Museum”.

    That the timing of the vote was already becoming a flashpoint in the caucus speaks to the rocky start for the incoming majority despite a near-sweep of key midterm races that could give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber.

    The prospect of an earlier vote had been floated as a way to prevent internal divisions from hobbling the incoming majority before the 120th Congress even began.

    Industry observers note that but supporters of Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., both in the chamber and among party activists outside it, were increasingly casting the idea of a shorter contest as a bid to halt momentum for his bid against Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y.

    Even as Schumer maintained that he has the votes necessary to be elected as majority leader, several senators insisted Tuesday the discussion taking place within the caucus was a good thing.

    “I’m confident I’ll be the next leader. I have the votes,” Schumer told reporters on Tuesday following the conference’s lunch.

    Van Hollen for his part told reporters Tuesday he believes his bid has “momentum at this point in time, which is why there was an effort to short-circuit the process.”.

    “And fortunately, I think that will fail.”.

    Several senators leaving the meeting said the topic of the leadership contest did not come up at all, and that neither Van Hollen nor Schumer gave a presentation regarding their bids.

    That was in large part due to the absence of the incoming senators — which could be as high as 13, depending on how the dust settles in Alaska — who are able to vote in the leadership elections. Retiring senators do not cast a ballot.

    With such a large class of incoming freshman, several incumbents saw it crucial to keep the election scheduled as is.

    “No one has ever raised that with me. I mean, I saw a rumor that some were wanting to contemplate that,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., noted Tuesday after the meeting. “The leadership discussions did not come up today. And part of the reason is we didn’t have the newcomers.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “Remember, they all get a vote in the leadership discussion, and it would be hard to get them here,” Kaine continued, noting that only Sen.-elect Scott Colom, D-Miss., was present for Tuesday’s lunch amid his belated orientation. “But nobody else was here, and that discussion needs to have the newcomers because newcomers get votes. The outgoers don’t, right?”.

    It has been revealed that sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M. echoed that sentiment on Monday evening, saying, “I want to hear from the freshman class as well.”.

    Sen. Mazie K. Hirono, D-Hawaii, said, “I don’t know that” when asked about moving up the elections. “I think that we need to make sure that there’s enough time for what I would call a robust discussion about what we’re going to do. I think we should be very embracing of the fresh people who have been through fire to get here, and I think that we have to make sure that all these voices are heard.

    “They’ve got a lot of talent to bring to the table,” she mentioned.

    Several senators-elect are among those who have publicly thrown their hats into Van Hollen’s corner, including Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.El-Sayed on Tuesday stated at The Atlantic Summit that he sees Van Hollen as “unique” in his experience in the Senate and running the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee as well as what he called “a willingness to take risks.”.

    “We need people who are willing to take legislative risk,” he stated. “We need to rethink the way we legislate. It just should not be the process where you make one or two omnibus pieces of legislation that nobody really knows what’s in them,” he continued, advocating for piecemeal legislation.

    Recent findings suggest that but there are about 15 Democrats who have publicly backed Schumer’s bid. If former Rep. Mary Peltola maintains her lead in the lone outstanding Senate race in Alaska, Schumer would need 29 to secure the helm of the ship.

    Industry observers note that “I committed to Sen. Schumer literally months ago, and I continue to support him,” Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said Monday. “I’m incredibly excited about the new ideas that our new colleagues have, and their energy, and the potential for changing the way we operate in the Senate, which we have to do because we need to be more effective.”.

    Sources indicate that several incumbents have also thrown their support behind Van Hollen for leadership change, including Sens. Jeff Merkley of Oregon and Bernie Sanders of Vermont.“I think, as I’ve remarked many times, the American people want change in the way we do business here in Washington, and I think Chris Van Hollen would be a great leader of the Democrats,” Sanders said Monday.

    Several senators and senators-elect are refusing to comment publicly on who they’ll back.

    In a recent development, that included Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who said he wants “to hear the commitments from folks that are pursuing this leadership role as well as every leadership position in the Senate, as well as chairs of committees, to what their commitments are to having a strong agenda that’s going to improve people’s lives.”.

    According to recent reports, kaine is also in that camp, and insisted Monday he hadn’t made up his mind. But he did speak positively of Schumer’s recruiting efforts in the midterms and history of dealing with a Trump White House.

    In a recent development, “Schumer just delivered a major win for us. No one who was not on the ballot worked harder for this victory than Chuck Schumer,” he said. “Chuck Schumer also happens to know Donald Trump better than anybody else in the caucus, and dealing with this wounded president is going to be a challenge over the next few years.”.

    “The voters are also overwhelmingly demanding change,” he said. “So we got to figure that out as a caucus, and we’re going to be able to. And we’re not afraid to have a discussion because we’re Democrats. We like democracy.”.

    According to recent reports, sen. John Hickenlooper, D-Colo., also remained mum on who he’ll support but remarked, “You can’t argue” Schumer brought Democrats the majority.

    “I think it’s a healthy thing to try and improve how the conference goes about its business,” he said. “I don’t think that is a distraction. We can deal with some distractions. We have to keep our eye on the ball.”.

    It has been revealed that sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., who last week called for fresh leadership in a news conference with Sanders, days before Van Hollen’s announcement, was noncommittal arriving to the Capitol on Monday if that meant she’d be supporting the Maryland Democrat.

    Senate Democrats’ election will most likely be a secret ballot. And most senators remained unified against moving the leadership elections before they recess for the Thanksgiving break.

    According to recent reports, “They should not be moved up. There was a reason that those rule changes took place before, and they should take place in December,” Lujan said.

    Kaine dismissed Van Hollen’s challenge as anything unusual.

    “We’re Democrats. It’s frankly unusual that there usually [aren’t] challenges to Democratic leaders because we’re Democrats,” he said. “It’s been a little unusual to have been here for 13 years and not really have them like this. But I think it’s a discussion not just about the two contenders for the leader role, but also the leadership team and priorities, and it’s all wrapped up in one discussion.”.

    “That’s why we decided, don’t do these votes until December, because you want to let the election settle and understand exactly what’s up, and then hear from potential votes.”.

    Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., mentioned, “I think we should stick with the rules when it comes to the caucus. … That’s going to be what makes sure that we show that we have a real process.”.

    Sanders asked: “Why would anyone want to do that?” when asked.

    “I think there’s a date that’s been called, and that should be the date.”.

    Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.
