    Influencer Uses AI To Score American First Class Upgrade… And Overpays

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1072 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • There’s no denying that AI holds a lot of potential to transform how we go about our every day life, both for better or worse.
    • Industry observers note that people are increasingly using AI for travel planning, but here’s an interesting twist on that.
    • Industry observers note that an Instagram user with 1.5 million followers who promises to help people master AI has just published a video about how “ChatGPT upgraded me to first class.” Now, that’s not as exciting as it sounds on the surface.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    There’s no denying that AI holds a lot of potential to transform how we go about our every day life, both for better or worse.

    Industry observers note that people are increasingly using AI for travel planning, but here’s an interesting twist on that. Can AI help you find award flights and secure upgrades? It’s something I’d like to study in a bit more detail and write about in the coming weeks, but I just saw a post on Instagram that piqued my interest, so I figured it would make for a fun story. Consider this just a little teaser, for the time being.

    Industry observers note that an Instagram user with 1.5 million followers who promises to help people master AI has just published a video about how “ChatGPT upgraded me to first class.” Now, that’s not as exciting as it sounds on the surface. The idea is simply that ChatGPT helped someone secure an upgrade through the standard means — it’s not like ChatGPT used his/her/their charm to sweet talk someone into an upgrade by dressing up nicely. 😉.

    Let me actually just quote the description of the video, which covers most of the content:.

    What happens when you ask ChatGPT to upgrade your flight to first class?

    I tried this on my flight in two weeks and it actually worked.

    Go to ChatGPT and switch from Chat to Work at the top. Start a new chat and give it your airline and confirmation code.

    Prompt 1:“Ask me every question you need about my credit cards, my miles, and my memberships, and map out every upgrade currency I own for this exact flight.”.

    ChatGPT shows you that you’ve been sitting on upgrade power this whole time without even knowing it.

    Prompt 2:“Now look up my exact flight, check how empty the first class cabin is, and tell me every way I can get up there, ranked from free to cheapest.”.

    In a recent development, prompt 3:“Now go get me the upgrade. Use my miles if the math is worth it, and place the upgrade bid at the smartest number, or get me on the upgrade list right now.”.

    ChatGPT opens its own browser, logs into your airline, and actually chases that seat for you while you sit back and do nothing.

    You can watch the video for yourself below.

    A post shared by Maverick Maltin | AI & ChatGPT (@mavgpt).

    I don’t want to suggest AI isn’t useful, but I’d say that the example given is actually very poor. First of all, let’s be clear about what’s actually going on here. He had booked a business class ticket on American from Los Angeles (LAX) to London (LHR), and then upgraded to first class.

    Now, in the first place, something isn’t fully accurate here:.

    Industry observers note that okay, maybe he edited the dates, or something, which is fine, and it’s besides the point, but as a detail oriented airline nerd, I couldn’t help but notice those things. Anyway, let’s assume this is all accurate:.

    To me, this is kind of where AI falls flat, and it isn’t the correct way to use it. The prompt was reportedly to “use my miles if the math is worth it, and place the upgrade bid at the smartest number, or get me on the upgrade list right now.” This is where I get confused — you’d think that AI would be able to scour reviews online, and see that American first class isn’t (well, or wasn’t) really viewed as a product that’s worth the premium.

    It has been revealed that if AI were really providing useful advice here, it would’ve recommend waitlisting with the systemwide upgrade, and otherwise recommending the guy save his 70,000 miles, and use them for something else. While there are definitely some strong use cases for AI, I think this is actually a pretty poor showing of what it can do.

    By the way, keep in mind that under United’s updated contract of carriage, using AI to help service reservations is banned, and could potentially get your ticket canceled. Whether there’s any enforcement of that remains to be seen.

    While the thought of using AI to score an upgrade might sound great, don’t count on it actually getting you the best deal. An AI whiz claims he has the secret to using AI to upgrade to first class. All AI did was use the instant upgrade offer that was available directly on American’s website, and it didn’t even encourage him to skip the upgrade due to it not being worthwhile, or waitlisting the upgrade with a systemwide upgrade, which is objectively a much better deal than 70,000 miles.

    What do you make of this AI “assistance” for a first class upgrade?

    Membership is free and takes no more information than commenting as a guest. Earn status points for good contributions, and see fewer ads as your status grows.

    Your feedback is important in helping us keep our community safe.

    The comments on this page have not been provided, reviewed, approved or otherwise endorsed by any advertiser, and it is not an advertiser's responsibility to ensure posts and/or questions are answered.

    Recent findings suggest that getting views and clicks are the primary motivation. Being truthful rarely is. Looks like he succeeded in views and clicks. That’s all it matters.

    Industry observers note that "Okay, maybe he edited the dates, or something, which is fine" - Nothing about that or any of his lies is fine. And why do you refer to him as an AI whiz without a "self-proclaimed" qualifier. He is quite the opposite.

    According to recent reports, what an abysmal ‘deal’ (assuming he actually went forward with paying that). I’ve managed to fly Flagship First from DFW-LHR for 65k miles outright in the past. And that doesn’t even account for the fact that AA’s mileage upgrade offers are usually a flat (roughly) 1 cent/mile toward the upgrade cost, which is terrible value. And the minimal difference between J and F on AA. Hell, Air France sometimes charges even less than that for a last minute upgrade between economy and business transatlantic.

    I bet he didn't actually spend the points + money, and made that part up for clicks.

    #88397. Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (771 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Mary Peltola unseats Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (771 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, former Alaska Rep.
    • Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen.
    • The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola speaks during her election night party in Anchorage on Nov. 3. (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images).

    Sources indicate that former Rep. Mary Peltola has defeated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska, giving Senate Democrats their ninth pickup of the midterm elections and bringing their caucus’s total seats in the next Congress to 56.

    The Associated Press called the race for Peltola around 10:19 p.m. Eastern time on Tuesday, a full two weeks after Election Day. The latest tranche of ballots counted put the former congresswoman past the 50-percent threshold to win the election outright without Alaska’s ranked choice voting system kicking in.

    With her victory, Peltola, who is Yup’ik, becomes one of the first Native American women elected to the Senate, along with fellow Democrat Peggy Flanagan, who won the open seat in Minnesota this month.

    “As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my life to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first.,” Peltola mentioned in a statement after the race was called.

    The Alaska race was the final Senate contest to be called in a midterm election that saw Democrats win commanding majorities in both chambers of Congress. Besides Alaska, Democrats also flipped Senate seats in North Carolina, Maine, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi.

    Peltola, a former state legislator, made history in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to Congress, winning a special election for the state’s at-large district. She comfortably won the general election that fall but was narrowly unseated in 2024 by Republican Nick Begich.

    Recent findings suggest that she entered the Senate contest in January, positioning herself as an independent-minded Democrat and invoking the legacies of two well-liked Alaska Republicans, the late Sen. Ted Stevens and the late Rep. Don Young, whom she succeeded in the House.

    She campaigned on the slogan “fish, family, freedom” and played up her moderate views and deep roots in the state.

    But the race was marked by allegations of political gamesmanship. In addition to the incumbent Sullivan, a retired colonel in the U.S. Marine Corps Reserves, the Senate ballot also included a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan. The Newly introduced York Times reported late last month that operatives aligned with Peltola’s campaign were involved in the effort to recruit the second Dan Sullivan in an attempt to confuse voters.

    Peltola has mentioned she had no connection to the scheme.

    According to recent reports, prior to Election Day, the Trump administration filed a lawsuit seeking to delay certification of the result if Sen. Sullivan were to lose. The lawsuit was tossed earlier this month by a federal judge.

    Trump also suggested that all votes cast for Dan J. Sullivan should be added to the incumbent’s total. “If you add them up, Dan Sullivan wins,” the president told reporters Monday. But as of Tuesday evening when the race was called, Peltola had more votes than both Sullivans combined.

    Recent findings suggest that the Alaska race was initially viewed as a long shot for Democrats. The Last Frontier has elected a Democratic senator just once in the past 50 years – in 2008, when Mark Begich ousted Stevens. Begich, the Democratic uncle of the current Republican congressman, served a single term before he was ousted by Sullivan in 2014.

    But anger in Alaska over the rising cost of food and fuel — already among the highest in the nation — provided Democrats with an opening.

    "56 seats was an unimaginable result even just a few months ago," Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer said in a statement Tuesday night. "But I knew if we concentrated on getting the best candidates, and if we focused like a laser on the costs, corruption, and chaos that Donald Trump has wrought throughout America, we would have shot.".

    In other Alaska races, Democrats flipped the governor’s mansion, with former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins winning an open-seat race to become the first Democrat elected governor of the state since Tony Knowles won a second term in 1998.

    According to recent reports, the race for the state’s at-large House district will be decided by ranked choice voting, with tabulations expected to take place Wednesday. Begich, the GOP incumbent, was leading Tuesday with 47.5 percent of the vote and is expected to prevail over independent Bill Hill, who had the backing of national Democrats and trailed with 42 percent. Another Democrat and a Libertarian combined for the remainder of the vote.

    #88389. The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1599 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    The Plot to Overthrow the Electoral College Must Fail

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, article II, Section 1 of the Constitution sets out the process by which Americans select their president.
    • Democrats have been railing against the Electoral College since losing the 2000 and 2016 elections while winning a plurality of the popular vote.
    • A proposed workaround has sailed through the legislatures of 18 blue states and the District of Columbia: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, article II, Section 1 of the Constitution sets out the process by which Americans select their president. Alexander Hamilton marveled at the time, in Federalist No. 68, that it was “almost the only part of the system, of any consequence, which has escaped without severe censure, or which has received the slightest mark of approbation from its opponents.” The core of that process is that the members of the Electoral College are selected in each state. With only the Twelfth Amendment’s modification in 1804 to adjust how the vice president is selected, this same system has been in continuous use for 238 years. It is how George Washington, Abraham Lincoln, Franklin D. Roosevelt, Ronald Reagan, and Barack Obama were elected. Now, a nefarious plot aims to overthrow the American system.

    Democrats have been railing against the Electoral College since losing the 2000 and 2016 elections while winning a plurality of the popular vote. These partisan sour grapes have often been dismissed as empty talk because the Electoral College is established by the Constitution, so only an amendment could abolish it. An amendment requires a two-thirds vote of Congress and the consent of 38 states, both of which are out of reach on a party-line vote.

    A proposed workaround has sailed through the legislatures of 18 blue states and the District of Columbia: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact. The theory is that these states would award their electors not to the winner of the popular vote in their own state, but to the winner of the national popular vote. It may be that a state can decide on its own to do this. States have not always picked electors by statewide popular vote. Many states at the Founding had their state legislatures choose electors. South Carolina did so all the way to the Civil War. Colorado in 1876 was the last state to do so, but only because it had just been admitted to statehood and claimed not to have time to organize a statewide vote. Other states have awarded electors to the winners of each House district, as Maine and Nebraska do today; this system was upheld by the Supreme Court in 1892.

    It has been revealed that but the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact is not just a unilateral decision by individual states about how to award their electors. If it had been, it would already have been effective in 2024, and Donald Trump would have won the Electoral College 530–8 with 49.7 percent of the popular vote. Instead, it is styled as an agreement that goes into effect only if states composing a majority of the Electoral College approve it. At present, the signatories control 222 electoral votes. With Democrats gaining trifectas in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada, and Arizona, they conceivably could pass the compact in states controlling 283 electoral votes. They also now control the Upcoming Hampshire state legislature, although with a veto-proof majority only in one of its two chambers, they would have to get through Republican Governor Kelly Ayotte.

    Passage is not certain. Michigan Democrats have previously rejected the compact in 2023 and 2024, and in Nevada (a smaller state that would be swamped under the compact), the Democratic governor vetoed it in 2019. Some of the small-state signatories, such as Delaware, Vermont, Rhode Island, or Upcoming Mexico, might yet have second thoughts now that they are playing with live ammunition.

    Industry observers note that moreover, under Article I, Section 10, interstate compacts require the consent of Congress. Even if Democrats passed it in the next two years with the aim of changing the rules for the 2028 election, Trump would surely veto it. After the 2030 Census, a number of the signatory states are expected to lose House seats, which will further narrow the margin for keeping it in effect. Then, there’s the question of whether the Supreme Court would allow individual states to gang up and effectively nullify the entire constitutional design of our presidential election system.

    It has been revealed that legal obstacles aside, this is a bad idea. To start with, the very durability of our system over such a long period is an argument in its favor. No other nation has used the same system for choosing its head of state and government for so long. Leaving aside the dubious precedents of 1824 (when popular vote records were not kept in the most populous state) and 1876 (when fraud was rampant in both parties and Southern Democrats engaged in mass violence against Republican voters), the Electoral College has only delivered a different outcome from the national popular vote three times in our history. In each case, the national vote was fairly close and neither candidate got a popular majority, so the Electoral College provided the legitimacy of a majority result that the popular vote could not. This may have frustrated Californians, but it was not just the tyranny of a few small places with no people in them. In 2016, Trump won the popular vote in seven of the ten largest states. It is nearly impossible to win a national popular majority without carrying the Electoral College.

    We have an Electoral College because we are a nation of diverse and distinct states. The American people are long accustomed to this system. The people ratified the Constitution and its amendments state-by-state. The Senate is elected by the people in states, the House by people in districts. Both political parties choose their presidential nominees by primary elections in each state. Americans have never before held a nationwide popular vote for any purpose. Our election systems, run by state and local officials with a variety of rules for the timing of casting and counting ballots and for confirming the qualifications of voters, are not designed for such a vote.

    Our campaigns today still prioritize appeals to the most closely divided states. This encourages presidential candidates to pitch at least some of their message to voters in the center, and also to travel the country in order to garner coverage in statewide media and the support of state and local power brokers. A national popular vote campaign would drive us even further down the road of nationalizing the campaign media environment and encouraging candidates to rally voters in their party’s strongholds. It would also exacerbate the divide between urban and rural or small-town America, given how the largest cities could effectively ally themselves against their own in-state neighbors.

    Few of the world’s democracies conduct a nationwide vote for the chief executive. In France, which is one of those, the first man to win such a vote seized power in a coup before his first term ended. National popular plebiscites are far more common in dictatorial systems, where the president has more control over who counts the votes. One of the reasons why the January 6 mob was never a serious threat to overturn the 2020 election was that the state-by-state winners had already been publicly certified in 50 separate state capitals. This was a deliberate feature of the system: As Hamilton wrote, “as the electors, chosen in each State, are to assemble and vote in the State in which they are chosen, this detached and divided situation will expose them much less to heats and ferments . . . than if they were all to be convened at one time, in one place.”.

    We would inevitably need to overhaul our entire election system to accommodate a nationwide vote. It is not a coincidence that such a nationalization of elections is favored by many of the same people who want to do away with the Electoral College. As things stand today, the whole country would have to wait on California, which not only takes weeks to count votes, but does so in order to count late-arriving ballots and to “cure” defective ballots — a process bound to erode confidence in a close election. That matters little when nobody doubts the outcome in California. But by making elections turn on the margins of victory in the deepest-blue or deepest-red jurisdictions, whose election officials are uniformly of the same party, the incentives for all manner of electoral malfeasance would be supercharged.

    The 1888 election provides a vivid, if extreme, example of how the Electoral College limits the scope of mischief done by the corruption of voting systems in particular states. The eleven states of the former Confederacy were then well into the post-Reconstruction suppression of the black vote in their states. As a result, the Democratic nominee, Grover Cleveland, won those states by almost 25 points, with over 60 percent of the vote. This propelled Cleveland to a narrow plurality in the national popular vote even though his Republican opponent, Benjamin Harrison, won a popular majority in the rest of the country. Yet the Electoral College gave Harrison the victory because his support was not as concentrated in an unrepresentative handful of states in which the vote was compromised.

    If a nationwide vote would be a headache, a nationwide recount would be a nightmare. Nobody who lived through the 2000 and 2020 post-election controversies should have any illusions that such a thing could be conducted in a civil and orderly fashion in today’s America. Rather than wait to learn that lesson the hard way, we should step back from the brink of overthrowing the system that has chosen our nation’s leader from the beginning.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

    Breaking: JSX Buys Newly introduced Pacific Airlines—42 Seat Jets Could Bring Its Private Terminal Flights To More Travelers

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2398 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that JSX has acquired New Pacific Airlines, and plans to bring the failed airline back with 42 seat Embraer regional jets.
    • I think this fits a firm that’s been unusually creative about finding markets and figuring out how to serve them.
    • Recent findings suggest that JSX is continually evaluating opportunities to support its long-term growth and bring its distinctive flying experience to more Customers and more communities.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that JSX has acquired New Pacific Airlines, and plans to bring the failed airline back with 42 seat Embraer regional jets. That’s 12 more seats than JSX sells on its planes today, and it gives them a way to grow beyond the limits of their current operation. I think this fits a organization that’s been unusually creative about finding markets and figuring out how to serve them. They brought turboprops to Santa Monica’s shortened runway and used a free membership program to gain access to Teterboro in order to serve New York. JSX isn’t laying out the New Pacific strategy yet. Asked about the deal, they tell me: JSX is continually evaluating opportunities to support its long-term growth and bring its distinctive flying experience to more Customers and more communities. As part of that work, we are pursuing additional pathways that could provide even more ways to deliver our award-winning service in the future. Our focus remains on the exceptional experience, convenience, and hospitality our Customers have come to expect from JSX. New Pacific has filed its intent to resume flying and requested a waiver of the usual 45 day advance filing requirement. An operating projection calls for: Embraer ERJ145-LR aircraft with 42 seats. Two aircraft initially, growing to six by the fifth month. 10,106 flights and roughly 309,000 passenger boardings in the first year. Flights averaging about 1.2 hours gate to gate, with staffing growing to 104 employees. New Pacific used to be Northern Pacific, the startup that wanted to connect the mainland U.S. and Asia through Anchorage using Boeing 757s. It seemed unlikely to work anyway but the closure of Russian airspace to U.S. carriers kept them from even trying. It pivoted to short domestic routes and then sports and corporate charters. I reported its shutdown last November, just two weeks after it unveiled an all-business class venture with beOnd. The bankruptcy process disposed of its 757s. What it has instead is Part 121 certification allowing operations beyond the 30 passenger limit of JSX’s current Part 135 public charter model. I first flew JSX home from Southwest Airlines Media Day in late 2022. JSX’s 4 p.m. departure got me home for dinner, an hour ahead of the Southwest flight I would have taken. I reached the terminal 19 minutes before departure. In Austin, I was in a Lyft less than ten minutes after touchdown. The plane was comfortable, with a seat on each side of the aisle and a side table next to mine. But getting my time back was what made it worth paying more (but honestly, not much more). I didn’t need a bigger airport lounge. I needed to spend less time at the airport. By my March 2023 visit to JSX’s headquarters, they’d fixed my one real complaint: no internet. JSX was the first carrier with Starlink, and the first to finish equipping its full fleet. Notably United Airlines owns a stake in JSX. The early JSX adoption is likely related to United’s head start with Starlink among major airlines. JSX’s business depended on putting several things together: inexpensive used aircraft, a comfortable cabin, friendly service and airports that let customers avoid wasting time. At the time, airport real estate was their biggest constraint. Finding another city with people willing to buy a ticket wasn’t enough. They needed somewhere to put the operation. Look at Santa Monica. The city is literally closing the airport and shortened its runway to 3,500 feet. JSX brought in ATR 42-600 turboprops configured with 30 seats. They found an aircraft suited to an airport that’s convenient for customers on the west side of Los Angeles, and obtained permission to operate despite the local politics. At Teterboro, the solution involved how they sold tickets. The airport prohibits publicly advertised scheduled passenger service. JSX put the flights behind a Club JSX login, limited bookings to members, and marketed the destination publicly as New York City. Joining the program is free, but joining is how they gain access to the airport. Those are different solutions to different problems. With New Pacific, JSX gains the ability to operate with more than 30 seats. My guess is that they see markets where a different version of their product could work, with more passengers sharing the cost of each departure. There is a regulatory insurance benefit. American Airlines, Southwest and the big pilots union have pushed to restrict JSX’s business model. I anticipated that sort of campaign in my first review. Having a Part 121 operation would be useful if the rules change. But the Federal Aviation Administration’s current agenda lists its public charter rulemaking as a long-term action with the next step undetermined. They never closed the rulemaking effort. But I think it’s possible to overread the regulatory risk insurance strategy here. They could still use private terminals with a part 121 operation and 42 seats. Federal security rules provide for scheduled and public charter flights with 31 to 60 seats outside the usual secure terminal area. This wouldn’t work at every airport JSX currently serves due to airport certification requirements. And part 121 means different pilot requirements, including mandatory age 65 retirement (they couldn’t use their ex-American and Southwest senior captains). If they do plan 42 seats that a different product – still more generous than a 50-seat sardine can but not nearly as spacious as the current 30-seat setup JSX appears to have a plan to add 40% more seats to some of the regional jets they own, and operate them under a scheduled airline. They haven’t remarked what they’re actually planning, but it may be a different niche than their current model rather than the assumed ‘buy a scheduled airline in case the next administration capitulates to lobbyists and puts them out of business’ the way ALPA, Southwest and American sought to do under the last administration.     #88385. LATAM Airlines unveils fresh A321XLR cabins with eye on US expansion

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (343 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thepointsguy ↗ Open Full Page

    LATAM Airlines unveils fresh A321XLR cabins with eye on US expansion

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (343 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The next frontier for the Airbus A321XLR is South America.
    • After opening dozens of upcoming transatlantic routes, the long-range narrow-body will make its debut with LATAM Airlines in March 2027.
    • It has been revealed that LATAM, a close partner of Delta Air Lines, will outfit its fleet of XLRs with 174 seats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The next frontier for the Airbus A321XLR is South America.

    After opening dozens of upcoming transatlantic routes, the long-range narrow-body will make its debut with LATAM Airlines in March 2027. The airline has yet to say which routes the XLRs will fly, but executives have previously outlined opportunities to connect the U.S. and South America.

    It has been revealed that LATAM, a close partner of Delta Air Lines, will outfit its fleet of XLRs with 174 seats. Business class will feature 12 lie-flat suites supplied by Thompson Aero Seating in a 1-1 layout with privacy doors.

    The suites include 19-inch personal entertainment screens, Bluetooth connectivity and in-seat charging options.

    Recent findings suggest that economy features 13-inch screens at each of the 126 seats, which are supplied by Recaro, plus Bluetooth connectivity and USB-C outlets. The cabin includes 36 extra-legroom seats.

    “The Airbus A321XLR allows us to take our value proposition to the next level and elevate the travel experience for our passengers,” said Paulo Miranda, the chief customer officer of LATAM, in a statement. He described the interior, which features red, orange and blue hues, as “inspired by South America.”.

    Industry observers note that LATAM executives have said it could fly the XLR on routes into the U.S. from its hub at Jorge Chavez International Airport (LIM) in Lima. However, those plans were called into question in May over the addition of a "connection fee" at LIM.

    The airline and Delta serve six U.S. destinations from LIM: Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Miami International Airport (MIA), John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), Orlando International Airport (MCO) and, since January 2026, Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC).

    LATAM did not comment on specific route plans for the XLR.

    Sources indicate that the XLR is the second latest airplane type for LATAM in as many years. The airline took delivery of its first Embraer E195-E2 in October. It will use the small jet to expand its feeder network in Brazil and support additional long-haul, intercontinental flying.

    #88384. Tech Report: United Nigeria Airlines Flew Passengers To The Wrong City—3 Years Later, Chairman Admits They Lied About It

    Tech Report: United Nigeria Airlines Flew Passengers To The Wrong City—3 Years Later, Chairman Admits They Lied About It

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2269 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that united Nigeria Airlines flew passengers to the wrong city and blamed the weather.
    • Industry observers note that I covered this incident on November 28, 2023, including the conflict between the pilot reportedly acknowledging a wrong flight plan and the airline insisting on a weather diversion.
    • Executive Chairman Obiora Okonkwo revisited the episode at the World Public Relations Forum in Abuja on November 17.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that united Nigeria Airlines flew passengers to the wrong city and blamed the weather. Three years later, they’re admitting it was all a lie. I covered this incident on November 28, 2023, including the conflict between the pilot reportedly acknowledging a wrong flight initiative and the airline insisting on a weather diversion. Now, Live and Let’s Fly flags the airline chairman’s admission that the passengers’ explanation was right. Executive Chairman Obiora Okonkwo revisited the episode at the World Public Relations Forum in Abuja on November 17. A dispatcher had entered the wrong destination in the paperwork. The pilots flew there. The flight attendants apparently believed they’d reached the city everyone bought tickets to. He described the weather explanation as “just a lie” and offered this advice: “The best way of public relations is to tell the truth, but tell it responsibly.” Passengers Were Welcomed To Abuja While Sitting In Asaba On November 26, 2023, flight 0504 left Lagos with passengers booked to Abuja, Nigeria’s capital. It landed in Asaba instead, about 200 miles away. This was United Nigeria Airlines, not United Airlines. Passengers reported that the flight attendants welcomed everyone to Abuja but then everyone discovered where they actually were. November 26, 2023 — Peacock (@dawisu) Another passenger shared video: We legit got scared sha. Laff wan kee me 😅 pic.twitter.com/sWxbnJeDna— Lord Macky (@AugustineMacky) November 26, 2023 The airline’s original statement blamed “poor destination weather”, said the pilot knew about the diversion, and attributed the confusion to an incorrect cabin announcement. The plane eventually continued to Abuja. The Investigation Uncovered The Truth The flight used an Airbus A320 operated by Bulgaria’s Fly2Sky for United Nigeria Airlines. Fly2Sky said at the time that United Nigeria had assigned it a Lagos–Asaba flight the previous day and hadn’t requested a change during the pilots’ preflight briefing. The Nigerian regulator identified failures well beyond one person entering a destination incorrectly. In its findings there was: Poor coordination between United Nigeria’s operations center and the company supplying the aircraft. No joint preflight briefing between the pilots and flight attendants. United Nigeria’s failure to monitor the leased aircraft through its operations center. Failure to follow the approved flight plan filed with air traffic control. The chairman story is about a dispatch error. The regulator, though, laid out several opportunities to prevent it. British Airways Has Done It, Too In March 2019, a British Airways flight scheduled from London City to Düsseldorf went to Edinburgh after the pilots received paperwork for the wrong destination. The passengers had bought a flight to Germany but the flight took them to Scotland. A few weeks later, Scandinavian Airlines sent a Copenhagen–Florence flight to Bologna. That was a deliberate decision made before departure because the pilots lacked the correct routing information for Florence. They flew to Bologna with plans to bus passengers onward. It’s just that they kept this information to themselves. And in August 2025, I covered AirAsia X passengers being welcomed to Incheon after their Kuala Lumpur flight landed at Seoul’s Gimpo airport, about 20 miles away. Here’s the Instagram video from that coverage: View the video shared by @rizalhakimm_punyer on Instagram AirAsia X said it had intentionally diverted for fuel because bad weather had caused congestion at Incheon. It acknowledged an incorrect cabin announcement, said the captain corrected it, and offered travel vouchers. Okonkwo also used his conference appearance to discuss a passenger upset that an advertised 11:30 a.m. flight had left at 11:20. He said he’d initially wanted to shout back, but instead responded, “I apologise for United Nigeria Airline leaving on time.” An airline chairman giving a speech about accurately convey what on-time means.     #88382. Latest Update: Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

    Latest Update: Britt bill would launch national office to combat financial fraud

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (497 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority.
    • Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S.
    • Recent findings suggest that the draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    A bill introduced by Sen. Katie Britt on Wednesday aims to combat a rising diversity of financial fraud by unifying the U.S. effort to fight it.

    Recent findings suggest that the draft bill would establish a National Office for Scam and Fraud Prevention in the White House that would coordinate federal, state and private sector efforts. It is aimed at ensuring that federal agencies, law enforcement, financial institutions, telecommunications and technology companies and other groups work together, according to an overview from Britt.

    The latest office would promote intelligence sharing across the public and private sectors, coordinate consumer education efforts and improve assistance for victims.

    Britt, R-Ala., stated the effort is needed because fraudsters operate nimbly utilizing social media while taking advantage of fragmented or disorganized responses from individual companies and government agencies.

    “This effort is about bringing everyone to the table and making sure our response keeps pace with the criminals who are exploiting new technologies and gaps between sectors,” she stated in a statement. “When we work together to identify threats earlier and share information more effectively, we can better protect American families and businesses.”.

    The office would develop a “lexicon of fraud” so that terms for different kinds of scams are standardized between various federal law enforcement agencies to promote a “whole-of-government response,” a Britt aide stated.

    The office also would work to broaden the approach to combating fraud beyond just having financial institutions reimburse victims. It would tap telecommunications and technology companies to address fraud at its source, such as rip-offs that start as text messages, social media posts or online advertisements.

    In a recent development, britt has made fighting elder financial abuse a priority. She is the sponsor of a bill that would allow state, local and tribal law enforcement agencies to use federal grant funding to investigate financial fraud, particularly scams targeted at the elderly.

    The measure highlights the prevalence of "pig butchering," a common technique where a predator cultivates a personal relationship with a victim over many months to extract the most cash.

    The House passed its version of the bill in September with overwhelming bipartisan support. The House sponsor is Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa.

    In a recent development, senior financial abuse also was the focus of a bill the House passed in an overwhelming 414-2 vote in June. The legislation, sponsored by Rep. Ann Wagner, R-Mo., would codify Securities and Exchange Commission guidance that permits mutual funds and their agents to postpone the sale of securities if there is a reasonable belief that financial exploitation of someone who is elderly or disabled is occurring.

    It's not clear whether the Senate will take action on these bills or Britt's by the end of the year.

    “If it doesn’t get through in the lame duck, it will continue to be a priority in the 120th [Congress],” the Britt aide said.

    Per Politico, the incoming speaker of the House, Hakeem Jeffries, wishes to massively increase federal entitlements:.

    Industry observers note that I’m sorry: What? What is Jeffries talking about? Have he and those praising him taken leave of their senses? The United States is $41 trillion in debt. The federal government is running annual deficits of $2 trillion. We paid more in interest last year than we spent on defense. Medicare is unsustainable as it is. Social Security is just six years away from mandatory benefit cuts. And the Democratic Party’s leader in the House wants to add a vast new spending program onto the pile. Do my eyes deceive me?

    Charles C. W. Cooke is a senior editor at National Review and the host of The Charles C. W. Cooke Podcast.
